lessons.title: Power BI essentials
lessons.summaryHtml:
Power BI is Microsoft’s tool for turning raw data into interactive reports. You build in Power BI Desktop (a free Windows app), publish to the Power BI service in the browser, and view on the mobile apps.

Every project follows the same flow: get data, transform it, model it, visualize it, publish it and share it. Publishing creates a semantic model (the data and calculations, once called a dataset) and a report in a workspace. From there you can pin tiles to a dashboard or package content as an app.

This track follows the PL-300 exam: prepare the data (25–30%), model the data (25–30%), visualize and analyze (25–30%), and manage and secure (15–20%).
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power BI is Microsoft’s tool for turning rows of data into charts and numbers people can understand. You point it at your data, tidy it up, link the tables together and drag visuals onto a page. People can then click on the charts to explore the data themselves.

Think of a restaurant. The raw data is the vegetables delivered in the morning. Power Query is the prep kitchen where you wash and chop. The model is the recipe that says how things combine. The report is the plate that reaches the customer. The Power BI service is the dining room where people come to eat.

Why it matters

Most organisations already collect plenty of data. The problem is that it sits in spreadsheets, databases and apps that nobody looks at together. Managers ask the same questions every week and someone rebuilds the same Excel chart by hand.

Power BI fixes this. You build the report once. It refreshes on a schedule, so the numbers stay current. Everyone looks at the same figures, and they can filter by campus, month or team without asking for a new chart. At the Campus Help Desk, this means the head of IT can see open tickets by campus every morning without waiting for an email.

How it works

1. Three places you use Power BI.

PartWhat it isMain job
Power BI DesktopA free app for WindowsBuild: get data, transform, model, design report pages
Power BI serviceThe website at app.powerbi.comShare: workspaces, dashboards, apps, refresh, security
Power BI mobile appsApps for phones and tabletsView reports and dashboards on the move

Desktop runs only on Windows. If you use a Mac, you need a Windows virtual machine or a cloud PC. The service can do some editing in the browser, but Desktop is the full authoring tool and the one the exam assumes.

2. The flow. Almost every Power BI project follows six steps:

  1. Get data from files, databases, online services or Dataverse.
  2. Transform it in Power Query: fix types, clean text, remove what you do not need.
  3. Model it: create relationships between tables and write measures in DAX, Power BI’s formula language.
  4. Visualize it: build report pages with charts, cards, tables and slicers.
  5. Publish the file from Desktop to a workspace in the service.
  6. Share it through workspace access, an app, links or embedding.

This track follows the same order. Lessons B.3 to B.5 cover getting and transforming data, B.6 to B.10 cover modelling, B.11 to B.13 cover visuals, and B.14 to B.15 cover the service.

3. The main items.

ItemWhat it holdsWhere it is made
Semantic modelTables, relationships, measures and security roles. It used to be called a dataset.Desktop, then published to the service
ReportOne or more pages of interactive visuals, built on one semantic modelDesktop or the service
DashboardOne page of tiles pinned from one or more reportsOnly in the service
WorkspaceA shared folder for models, reports, dashboards and moreThe service
AppA read-only package of workspace content for a wide audienceThe service, published from a workspace

When you publish a .pbix file, the service splits it into two items: a semantic model and a report. Many reports can share one semantic model.

4. Views in Desktop. The icons on the left switch between views. Report view is where you build pages. Table view (called Data view in older versions) shows the loaded rows. Model view shows tables and relationships. DAX query view lets you run DAX queries. Power Query Editor opens in its own window when you choose Transform data.

5. Licences in general terms. Desktop is free. Anyone can build and save reports locally. Publishing to your own personal area of the service is possible with a free licence. Sharing content with other people generally needs a Pro or Premium Per User licence, or a workspace that sits on a paid capacity. Some features, such as Copilot in Power BI, need a paid capacity. A free trial is often available. Prices and exact rules change, so check Microsoft’s current licensing page before buying.

Remember: Dashboards exist only in the Power BI service. You cannot build a dashboard in Desktop.

Example: Campus Help Desk

In the PL-900 track you built a Help Desk with a Ticket table and a Category table. This track uses the same idea as two CSV files, so you can practise without a Dataverse licence.

  1. Copy tickets.csv (60 tickets from January to June 2026) and categories.csv (four categories) from the dataset panel.
  2. In Desktop choose Get data, then Text/CSV, and pick tickets.csv. A preview opens. It shows columns such as TicketID, CreatedDate, Priority, Status, Campus and AssignedTo.
  3. The preview offers Load and Transform data. Load brings the data straight in. Transform data opens Power Query first. For now, choose Load.
  4. Load categories.csv the same way. In Model view you may see a line between the two tables on CategoryID. Desktop sometimes detects relationships automatically.
  5. Add a Card visual showing the count of TicketID. It shows 60.
  6. Add a clustered bar chart with Campus on the axis and the count of TicketID as the value. Look closely: you may see more than three campuses, because some rows say "north" or have extra spaces. Lesson B.4 fixes that.

Later lessons turn this quick start into a proper star schema with a Date table, clean data, measures, secure sharing and scheduled refresh.

The PL-300 exam at a glance

PL-300 is the exam for the Microsoft Certified: Power BI Data Analyst Associate certification. The passing score is 700. Associate certifications are renewed every year with a free online assessment on Microsoft Learn. A free practice assessment is also available there.

AreaWeightLessons
Prepare the data25–30%B.3, B.4, B.5
Model the data25–30%B.6 to B.10
Visualize and analyze the data25–30%B.11, B.12, B.13
Manage and secure Power BI15–20%B.14, B.15

Common mistakes

  • Calling a report a dashboard. A report can have many pages and lives in Desktop and the service. A dashboard is one page of pinned tiles, only in the service.
  • Still saying "dataset". Microsoft now says semantic model. The exam uses the new name.
  • Thinking Desktop is paid. Desktop is free. Licences matter when you share in the service.
  • Emailing .pbix files around. That breaks security and refresh. Publish to a workspace and share there.
  • Choosing Load when data is messy. If the preview shows problems, choose Transform data and clean first.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Single page", "pinned", "tiles from several reports" point to a dashboard in the service.
  • "Distribute to many users who only view" points to an app published from a workspace.
  • "Collaborate with colleagues who build content" points to a workspace with the right roles.
  • "Reuse the same data for several reports" points to one shared semantic model.

A single page of tiles pinned from reports. Exists only in the Power BI service.

options: A dashboard in the Power BI service
A new page in Power BI Desktop
quiz.explanation: A dashboard is a single page of tiles pinned from one or more reports. Dashboards exist only in the Power BI service.

options: A semantic model and a report
quiz.explanation: Publishing a .pbix file creates a semantic model (the data and model) and a report (the pages of visuals). Dashboards and apps are created separately.

options: Install the Mac version from the App Store
Use the Power BI mobile app instead
Desktop cannot be used for authoring
Run Desktop in a Windows virtual machine or cloud PC
quiz.explanation: Power BI Desktop runs only on Windows. Mac users need a Windows VM or a cloud PC, or they can do limited authoring in the service.

options: Give every person the Admin role
Publish an app from the workspace
Create a new workspace per person
quiz.explanation: An app packages content from a workspace and distributes it to many viewers in a read-only, curated way.

lessons.title: Power BI and the Power Platform
lessons.summaryHtml:
Power BI is the analytics part of the Power Platform. It works closely with the other products.

  • Dataverse: Power BI connects to Dataverse tables, such as the Help Desk Ticket table, with a built-in connector.
  • Power Apps visual: puts a canvas app inside a report so users can act on the data they are looking at.
  • Power Automate: the Power Automate visual runs a flow from a report button; flows can also refresh a semantic model or react to a data alert.
  • Embedding: reports and tiles can appear inside Power Apps and as tabs in Microsoft Teams.

Together they close the loop: see a problem in a report, then fix it without leaving the page.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power BI is one member of the Power Platform family. Power Apps builds apps, Power Automate runs flows, Copilot Studio builds agents, and Dataverse stores data. Power BI is the member that helps people see what is happening.

On its own, a report only shows things. Joined with the other products, it lets people act. Picture a car dashboard with a warning light. Power BI is the warning light. Power Apps and Power Automate are the buttons that let you fix the problem without stopping the car.

Why it matters

In many companies, people read a report, spot a problem, then open a different system to fix it. They copy IDs by hand and switch between tabs. It is slow and mistakes happen.

When Power BI works with the rest of the platform, the whole loop happens in one place. A staff member sees an overdue high-priority ticket in the report, reassigns it from a small app inside the same page, and a flow emails the new owner. The report refreshes and the ticket drops off the overdue list.

How it works

1. Reading Dataverse data. Power BI has a Dataverse connector in Get data. You sign in with your work or school account, choose the environment, and pick tables such as Ticket and Category. Dataverse security still applies, so users see only rows they are allowed to see in Dataverse when the connection uses their identity. Choice columns such as Priority come through with their values and labels.

2. The Power Apps visual. This visual puts a canvas app inside a report. You add the visual, drag in the fields the app needs, and create or pick an app. The report passes the rows in the current filter context to the app. Inside the app, those rows are available as a special data source:

PowerBIIntegration.Data

When a user clicks a bar or a slicer in the report, the app receives the new set of rows. The app can then write back to Dataverse, for example to change a ticket’s status.

3. The Power Automate visual. This visual adds a button to the report. You drag in the data fields and build a flow for it. When a user clicks the button, the flow runs and receives the data currently in context. Typical uses: email a list of overdue tickets, post a message in Teams, or create a task.

4. Power Automate working with the service. The Power BI connector in Power Automate offers useful actions and triggers:

  • An action to refresh a semantic model. A flow can load new data and then start a refresh, instead of waiting for the schedule. Some screens still call it a dataset.
  • A trigger for data-driven alerts. You set an alert on a dashboard tile, such as a card, KPI or gauge. When the value crosses your threshold, the flow runs.
  • Actions to export reports and to add rows to certain kinds of semantic models.

5. Embedding Power BI elsewhere.

WhereHowWhat users see
Canvas appThe Power BI tile controlOne tile from a dashboard in the service
Model-driven appPower BI embedding, once enabled for the environmentPower BI reports or dashboards alongside Dataverse data
Microsoft TeamsA Power BI tab in a channel or chat, or the Power BI app in TeamsAn interactive report inside the conversation

In every case, the viewer still needs permission to see the Power BI content and the right licence. Embedding does not bypass security.

6. Which tool for which job.

NeedBest fit
Edit or update records from inside a reportPower Apps visual
Run an action with one click from a reportPower Automate visual
React automatically when a number passes a limitData alert on a dashboard tile plus a flow
Refresh the model right after new data arrivesFlow with the refresh action
Show a live chart inside an appPower BI tile in a canvas app, or embedding in a model-driven app
Discuss a report with a teamPower BI tab in Teams
Watch out: Data alerts are set on dashboard tiles in the service, and only on some tile types such as cards, KPIs and gauges. You cannot set them on a report visual in Desktop.

Example: Campus Help Desk

In the PL-900 track, tickets live in the Dataverse Ticket table. Staff use the "Help Desk Staff" model-driven app, and flows notify people. Here is how Power BI joins in.

  1. Connect. In Desktop, Get data, Dataverse. Choose the Help Desk environment and load Ticket and Category. (In this track we use the CSV copies instead, so everyone can follow along.)
  2. Report. Build a page showing open tickets by campus and priority.
  3. Act from the report. Add a Power Apps visual with Ticket ID, Status and Assigned to. The app lists the tickets in the current selection and has a button that reassigns the selected ticket in Dataverse.
  4. Escalate with one click. Add a Power Automate visual labelled "Email overdue list". Its flow sends the filtered tickets to the campus team lead.
  5. Alert. Publish, pin the "Open high-priority tickets" card to a dashboard, and set a data alert above a threshold you choose. A flow triggered by the alert posts to the IT team’s Teams channel.
  6. Share where people work. Add the report as a tab in the Help Desk Teams channel, and embed it in the "Help Desk Staff" model-driven app.

The result: staff see, decide and act without switching systems.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking reports can edit data by themselves. Visuals only read. Write-back needs the Power Apps visual or a flow.
  • Setting alerts on report visuals. Alerts belong to dashboard tiles in the service.
  • Assuming embedding shares the report. Viewers still need access and a suitable licence.
  • Mixing up the two visuals. Power Apps visual = an app with screens and forms. Power Automate visual = a button that runs a flow.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Update records without leaving the report" points to the Power Apps visual.
  • "Button in the report that sends an email or starts a process" points to the Power Automate visual.
  • "Notify when a value exceeds a threshold" points to a data alert on a dashboard tile, optionally triggering a flow.
  • "Refresh as soon as a load finishes" points to a flow using the refresh action.

quiz.explanation: The Power Apps visual embeds a canvas app in the report. It receives the filtered rows and can write back to Dataverse.

Through the Dataverse connector in Get data

domains.name: Prepare the data
domains.blurb: Connect to sources, profile and clean data, and shape it with Power Query.

lessons.title: Get and connect to data
lessons.summaryHtml:
Every report starts with Get data. Power BI connects to files, databases, online services, Dataverse, Fabric items and existing shared semantic models.

For each source you choose a storage mode:

  • Import copies data into the model. Fastest queries, needs refresh.
  • DirectQuery leaves data at the source and queries it live. Always current, usually slower.
  • Direct Lake reads Delta tables in Microsoft Fabric OneLake directly. Needs Fabric.

Data source settings hold credentials and privacy levels. Parameters let you change values such as a file path or server name without editing every query.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Before you can analyse anything, Power BI must reach your data. Get data is the front door. Behind it are hundreds of connectors: files like CSV and Excel, databases like SQL Server, online services like SharePoint, Dataverse, Microsoft Fabric, and other Power BI semantic models.

Connecting is only half the decision. You also choose how Power BI holds the data. Think of reading a library book. You can borrow it and take it home (Import). You can sit in the library and read it there every time (DirectQuery). Or the library can give you a fast reading room right next to the shelves (Direct Lake).

Why it matters

The wrong choice causes real pain. A report that imports a huge, fast-changing table may be out of date and slow to refresh. A report that uses DirectQuery against a busy database may be slow for every click. Hard-coded file paths break the day someone moves a folder. Wrong privacy settings can block a query or, worse, send private data to a public source.

The PL-300 exam spends a lot of attention here, because good choices at this step make every later step easier.

How it works

1. Connecting. In Desktop, choose Get data, pick a connector, and give it what it needs: a file path, a server and database name, a URL or an environment. Then sign in. You see a preview and choose Load or Transform data.

2. Connecting to a shared semantic model. If a colleague has already published a clean, trusted model, you do not need to rebuild it. Choose Get data, Power BI semantic models, and pick it. By default this is a live connection: you build report pages, but the model belongs to someone else, so you cannot change its tables. If you need to add your own data too, you can turn it into a composite model that mixes the shared model with local tables. Reusing one certified model keeps everyone on the same numbers.

3. Storage modes.

ModeWhere data livesStrengthsTrade-offsChoose when
ImportCopied into the semantic modelFastest visuals, all DAX and Power Query featuresNeeds refresh; data is only as fresh as the last refresh; model size limits applyMost reports; small to medium data; best performance
DirectQueryStays in the sourceNear real-time; very large data; no copy storedSlower visuals; load on the source; some transformation and DAX limitsData too big or changes too often to import, or must not be copied
Direct LakeDelta tables in Microsoft Fabric OneLakeImport-like speed without full import refreshesNeeds Microsoft Fabric and data in OneLakeYour organisation already stores data in Fabric
DualBoth imported and available as DirectQueryLets dimension tables work well with either kind of fact tableAdds complexityComposite models with mixed modes

You can check or change a table’s storage mode in Model view, in the table’s advanced properties. Some changes cannot be reversed, so save a copy first.

4. Data source settings. In Desktop, choose File, Options and settings, Data source settings. Here you can:

  • Change source to point to a new file or server.
  • Edit permissions to update credentials (for example switch from Windows to organisational account) or clear them.
  • Set the privacy level for each source.
Privacy levelMeaning
PrivateSensitive data. It is isolated and not sent to other sources.
OrganizationalCan be combined with other organisational sources, but not sent to public ones.
PublicAnyone could see it, such as open data on a website.
NoneNo level set. Power Query treats it cautiously and may warn you.

Privacy levels matter when one query combines two sources. Power Query may push values from one source into a request to another. Privacy levels stop private data leaking into, say, a public web request.

5. Parameters. A parameter is a named value in Power Query, such as a folder path, server name or date. You create one with Manage parameters, then use it inside queries. Change the value once and every query that uses it follows. Parameters are also handy for moving between test and production sources, and they can be changed in the service settings for the semantic model after publishing.

Remember: Import = speed, needs refresh. DirectQuery = fresh and big, slower. Direct Lake = Fabric OneLake.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Your two CSV files sit in a folder on your PC. Next term they will move to a shared SharePoint folder. You prepare for that now.

  1. Open Power Query with Transform data. Choose Manage parameters, New parameter. Name it DataFolder, type Text, value C:\Users\you\Documents\HelpDesk\.
  2. Open the tickets query in Advanced Editor. The first step reads the file. Change it to use the parameter:
Source = Csv.Document(
    File.Contents(DataFolder & "tickets.csv"),
    [Delimiter=",", Encoding=65001, QuoteStyle=QuoteStyle.Csv]
)
  1. Do the same for categories. Close & Apply. The report works exactly as before.
  2. Open Data source settings. You see the local folder source with Windows credentials. Set its privacy level to Organizational, because help desk data is internal.
  3. Check storage mode in Model view: both tables are Import. With only 60 tickets, Import is the right choice: fast, simple and fully featured.
  4. Imagine the university later stores tickets as Delta tables in Fabric OneLake. At that point Direct Lake would be worth considering. If tickets stayed in a large, busy SQL database and staff needed live counts, DirectQuery would be the candidate.

Common mistakes

  • Using DirectQuery "just to be safe". It is usually slower and limits features. Import is the default for good reasons.
  • Thinking Direct Lake works anywhere. It needs Microsoft Fabric and data in OneLake.
  • Setting every privacy level to None to silence warnings. The warnings exist to protect data.
  • Hard-coding paths and server names. Use parameters so changes happen in one place.
  • Rebuilding a model that already exists. Connect to the shared semantic model instead.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Real time", "billions of rows", "must not be copied" point to DirectQuery.
  • "Best performance", "small data", "offline analysis" point to Import.
  • "Fabric", "lakehouse", "OneLake", "Delta tables" point to Direct Lake.
  • "Server name changes between test and production" points to a parameter.
  • "Credentials expired" or "combine private and public data" points to data source settings.

terms.definition: Data is copied into the semantic model and refreshed on a schedule.
Data stays in the source; each visual sends queries to it at view time.
A Fabric storage mode that reads Delta tables in OneLake without a full import.
A setting (Private, Organizational, Public, or None) that controls whether data from one source may be combined with another.
A named value in Power Query, such as a folder path, used inside queries and changeable in one place.

lessons.examTip: “Near real-time from a large SQL database” points to DirectQuery; “data already in Fabric OneLake” points to Direct Lake; “fastest performance, small data” points to Import.

steps: Download parameter-queries.txt and keep tickets.csv and categories.csv in one folder.
Open HelpDesk.pbix and choose Transform data to open Power Query Editor.
Choose Manage parameters, then New parameter. Name it DataFolder, type Text, and set its value to the folder that holds your CSV files, ending with a backslash.

Select the tickets query, open Advanced Editor, and replace the hard-coded path in File.Contents with DataFolder & "tickets.csv", as in parameter-queries.txt. Do the same for categories with "categories.csv".
Test the parameter: set DataFolder to a folder that does not exist and select the tickets query, read the error, then set it back to the right folder.
Choose Close & Apply. Then choose File, Options and settings, Data source settings. Select your folder source and look at Edit Permissions to see the credential type and privacy level.
In Model view, select the tickets table and open its Advanced properties. Confirm the Storage mode is Import.
Choose Get data, then Power BI semantic models. Note that this connects live to a published model; close the window without connecting.
check: With the correct DataFolder, tickets still loads 60 rows and 9 columns, and categories 4 rows.
With a wrong DataFolder, the tickets query shows a DataSource.Error saying the file or path could not be found.
The Source step of both queries contains DataFolder & and no hard-coded folder.
The tickets table Storage mode is Import.

quiz.question: A sales database holds hundreds of millions of rows and changes every minute. Managers need current figures and the data must not be copied. Which storage mode fits?
quiz.explanation: DirectQuery keeps data at the source and queries it live, so figures are current and no copy is stored in the model.

quiz.question: Your company stores its tables as Delta tables in Microsoft Fabric OneLake. You want high performance without scheduled import refreshes. What should you choose?
quiz.explanation: Direct Lake reads Delta tables in OneLake directly. It needs Microsoft Fabric and avoids full import refreshes.

quiz.question: You move the Help Desk CSV files to a new folder. Ten queries use the old path. What makes future moves quick?
options: Create a parameter for the folder path and use it in every query
quiz.explanation: A parameter stores the path in one place. Queries reference it, so you change one value instead of ten queries.

quiz.question: A query combines a private HR file with a public web page and Power BI shows a privacy warning. Where do you review this setting?
quiz.explanation: Data source settings hold credentials and privacy levels for each source. Privacy levels control whether sources can be combined.

lessons.title: Profile and clean data
lessons.summaryHtml:
Before you model data, you check it. Power Query’s data profiling tools show quality, distribution and statistics for each column.

  • Column quality: percent valid, error and empty.
  • Column distribution: count of distinct and unique values.
  • Column profile: statistics and a value chart for one column.

By default, profiling uses only the first 1,000 rows; switch to the entire dataset in the status bar. Then fix what you find: Trim and Capitalize text, Replace values, handle nulls, and remove or replace errors. Every fix is saved as an applied step and runs again on each refresh.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Real data is messy. Names are typed in different ways, values are missing, and some cells hold text where numbers belong. If you load mess, your charts show mess.

Profiling means looking at your data before you trust it. Cleaning means fixing what you find. Think of a teacher marking exam papers. First they skim the pile to spot problems: missing names, pages out of order. Then they fix each problem the same way every time. Power Query does both jobs, and it remembers every fix so it can repeat it on the next refresh.

Why it matters

Small data problems cause big reporting errors. If some rows say "North", some say "north" and some say "North " with a space, a chart shows three campuses instead of one. Totals split across fake categories. Managers make decisions on wrong numbers.

Errors also break refresh. A single bad value in a number column can stop the whole semantic model from updating in the service. Catching these problems in Power Query, once, saves hours of fixing reports later.

How it works

1. Profiling tools. In Power Query Editor, the View tab has three data preview options.

ToolShowsHelps you spot
Column qualityPercent Valid, Error and Empty under each headerMissing values and conversion errors
Column distributionA small chart plus counts of distinct and unique valuesUnexpected variants, duplicates, possible keys
Column profileFull statistics (count, errors, empty, distinct, min, max and more) and a value chart for the selected columnOutliers, odd ranges, typos

Distinct means how many different values appear. Unique means how many values appear exactly once. A key column such as TicketID should have distinct = unique = row count.

Watch out: By default, profiling looks only at the first 1,000 rows. Click the text in the status bar at the bottom and choose profiling based on the entire dataset to see every row.

2. Column properties and types. Each column has a data type shown by an icon in the header: text, whole number, decimal number, date, true/false and others. Power Query often detects types automatically for CSV files. Always check them. A wrong type can turn good values into errors, or keep numbers as text so they cannot be summed.

3. Fixing inconsistent text.

  • Trim removes spaces at the start and end.
  • Clean removes non-printing characters such as hidden line breaks.
  • Format changes case: lowercase, UPPERCASE or Capitalize Each Word.
  • Replace values swaps one value for another, such as "Ntwk" for "Network".

These are on the Transform tab under Format, or by right-clicking the column header.

4. Nulls and blanks. A null is an empty value. Before replacing it, ask what it means. Sometimes a null is an error, such as a missing campus. Sometimes it is meaningful, such as no closed date on an open ticket. Useful tools:

  • Replace values to swap null for a default, only when a default makes sense.
  • Fill down or Fill up when a value is written once and should apply to the rows below.
  • Remove empty in a column filter to drop rows that should not exist.

5. Errors. An error cell means Power Query could not process that value, for example "n/a" in a whole-number column. You have three choices.

ActionEffectUse when
Keep errorsShows only the error rowsYou want to investigate the cause
Remove errorsDeletes rows with errors in the selected columnsThose rows are genuinely bad and not needed
Replace errorsPuts a value, often null, in place of each errorYou must keep the row but the value is unusable

6. Import errors. Some errors appear only when you choose Close & Apply. Desktop reports how many rows had errors and offers to show them. Common causes: a type change that fails on a few rows, a renamed or missing column in the source file, or a moved file. Go back to Power Query, find the failing step in Applied steps, and fix it there.

7. Applied steps. Every action becomes a step in the Applied steps list. Steps run in order on every refresh. You can rename, reorder or delete them. Clear step names help the next person understand your work.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The tickets.csv file has some deliberate problems. Here is how you find and fix them.

  1. Open Transform data and select the tickets query. Turn on Column quality, Column distribution and Column profile. Switch profiling to the entire dataset.
  2. TicketID: 60 distinct, 60 unique, 100% valid. Good: it can be the key.
  3. Campus: the distribution shows more than three values. The profile reveals variants such as "north" and "City " with a trailing space.
  4. Select Campus, choose Format, Trim, then Format, Capitalize Each Word. Distinct drops to 3: North, South, City.
  5. Priority: one row says "high". Apply Capitalize Each Word. Now only Low, Medium and High remain.
  6. ClosedDate and HoursToResolve: Column quality shows some Empty. Filter Status to Open and In progress: those rows are the empty ones. The nulls are correct, so you leave them alone.
  7. Check types: CreatedDate and ClosedDate as Date, HoursToResolve as Decimal number, CategoryID as Whole number.
  8. Rename the steps, for example "Clean Campus text" and "Clean Priority case". Choose Close & Apply.

Behind the scenes, Power Query writes M code. The Campus fix looks like this:

#"Clean Campus text" = Table.TransformColumns(
    #"Changed Type",
    {{"Campus", each Text.Proper(Text.Trim(_)), type text}}
)

Your bar chart of tickets by campus now shows exactly three bars.

Common mistakes

  • Trusting profiling on 1,000 rows. Problems deeper in the file stay hidden until refresh fails.
  • Replacing every null with 0. A missing resolution time is not zero hours. It would drag averages down.
  • Removing errors without looking. Keep errors first to understand the cause; you may be deleting real data.
  • Cleaning in the report instead of Power Query. Fix data once at the source step so every visual benefits.
  • Leaving default step names. "Changed Type1" tells nobody anything.

How the exam asks about it

  • "Percentage of empty or error values" points to Column quality.
  • "How many distinct values" or "find duplicates" points to Column distribution; "min, max, statistics" points to Column profile.
  • "Issue not visible in the preview" points to profiling the entire dataset.
  • "Keep the rows but hide bad values" points to Replace errors; "drop bad rows" points to Remove errors.
  • "Same value typed differently" points to Trim, Clean, Format or Replace values.

lessons.title: Transform and shape data
lessons.summaryHtml:
Once your data is clean, you shape it in Power Query so it fits a good model. You set the right data types, add new columns, group rows, and reshape tables with pivot, unpivot and transpose. You turn semi-structured data such as JSON into a normal table.

  • Merge joins two queries side by side on a key. Append stacks rows from queries with the same columns.
  • A reference query starts from the output of another query. A duplicate copies all its steps into an independent query.
  • You split data into fact tables (events you count) and dimension tables (things you describe), and you can turn off Enable load for helper queries.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Cleaning fixes what is wrong in your data. Transforming changes its shape so it fits the questions you want to answer. You do both in the Power Query Editor, before data reaches the model.

Think of a kitchen. Cleaning is washing the vegetables. Transforming is chopping them into the right sizes for the dish. The raw ingredients are the same, but the shape is now useful.

Every change you make becomes an applied step. Power Query writes each step in a language called M. When the data refreshes, Power Query replays the steps in order. You do the work once; it repeats forever.

Why it matters

Data rarely arrives in the shape a report needs. A survey may have one column per campus. A web API may return nested JSON. Monthly exports may sit in twelve separate files. If you load these as they are, your measures become complicated and your visuals become slow.

Shaping data early keeps the model simple. A good rule used by Power BI professionals is: “shape in Power Query, calculate in DAX”. Work that can be done once at refresh should not be repeated in every visual.

How it works

1. Data types. Every column needs the right type. Dates must be Date, hours must be a number, IDs used as keys should be Whole number. Wrong types cause sorting problems, failed relationships and measures that cannot sum. Set types deliberately, usually as an early step. Power Query often detects types automatically, but always check the result.

2. Creating columns. You have several options on the Add Column tab.

OptionWhat it doesHelp Desk use
Conditional columnIf-then-else rules built with a formIsClosed = Yes when Status is Closed
Custom columnA formula you write in MDays open = ClosedDate minus CreatedDate
Column from examplesYou type a few sample results and Power Query guesses the formulaExtract the month name from CreatedDate
Split, merge, extractBreak or combine text columnsSplit a “Campus - Building” value into two columns

3. Group and aggregate. Group By collapses rows into summary rows, for example one row per Campus with a count. This reduces detail, so only use it when you truly do not need the detail rows in the model.

4. Pivot, unpivot and transpose.

OperationEffectWhen to use
UnpivotMany columns become attribute and value rows (wide to long)One column per month or per campus; the most common fix
PivotValues in one column become new column headers (long to wide)Rarely for models; sometimes for a lookup layout
TransposeRows become columns and columns become rowsData typed sideways in a spreadsheet

5. Semi-structured data. JSON and XML contain records (one object with fields) and lists (many items). In Power Query they appear as clickable Record or List values. You use To Table and the expand button on a column header to turn them into ordinary rows and columns.

6. Fact and dimension tables. A fact table holds events, such as one row per ticket. A dimension table describes things, such as categories or staff members. You can build a dimension from a fact by referencing it, keeping the descriptive column and removing duplicates. Each dimension needs a key: a column with a unique value per row that the fact table also contains.

7. Reference versus duplicate.

ReferenceDuplicate
SourceThe output of the original queryA full copy of all the original steps
Changes to the originalFlow through automaticallyDo not affect the copy
Typical useBuild several tables from one cleaned staging queryExperiment or create a variant that must stay independent

8. Merge and append. Merge works like a join: it matches rows on key columns and adds columns from the second query. You choose a join kind, such as left outer (keep all rows from the first query) or inner (only matching rows). Append stacks rows from queries that share the same columns, such as January and February exports.

9. Configure loading. Each query has Enable load. Turn it off for helper or staging queries that feed other queries but should not appear in the model. There is also an option to include or exclude a query from report refresh.

Remember: in a star schema you usually do not merge dimension columns into the fact table. You keep them in separate tables and link them with relationships.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Open Transform data. In Tickets, set types: TicketID and CategoryID to Whole number, CreatedDate and ClosedDate to Date, HoursToResolve to Decimal number. Empty ClosedDate and HoursToResolve cells become null, which is correct for open tickets.
  2. Add a conditional column IsClosed. Power Query writes an M step similar to this: 
    = Table.AddColumn(#"Changed Type", "IsClosed",
    each if [Status] = "Closed" then "Yes" else "No")
  3. Right-click Tickets and choose Reference. Name it Agents. Keep only AssignedTo and remove duplicates. You now have a small dimension with one row per staff member, and it follows any future changes to Tickets.
  4. Imagine a second file, tickets-july.csv, with the same columns. You would load it, then use Append queries to stack it under Tickets.
  5. To see tickets per campus quickly, a Group By step would look like this: 
    = Table.Group(#"Added IsClosed", {"Campus"},
    {{"TicketCount", each Table.RowCount(_), Int64.Type}})
    You would do this in a separate referenced query, not in Tickets, because the model needs the detail rows.
  6. Leave Categories as its own dimension. Do not merge it into Tickets; the relationship in lesson B.6 will connect them.

Common mistakes

  • Confusing merge and append. Merge adds columns by matching keys. Append adds rows from similar tables.
  • Thinking a duplicate stays in sync. Only a reference follows changes to the original query.
  • Grouping the fact table and losing detail that later visuals need.
  • Pivoting when the data needs unpivoting. Models prefer long, narrow tables.
  • Loading every staging query into the model, which adds clutter and memory use.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Files with the same structure each month” or “combine rows” points to append. “Add the category name from another table using CategoryID” points to merge.
  • “One column per month or per region” and “need a single column to filter” points to unpivot.
  • “Changes to the first query must be reflected” points to reference. “Must not be affected” points to duplicate.
  • “Query is used only by other queries” or “should not appear in the model” points to clearing Enable load.
  • “JSON with nested records” points to converting to a table and expanding columns.

quiz.explanation: Unpivot turns several columns into attribute and value pairs, making the table long and easy to filter.

domains.name: Model the data
domains.blurb: Star schemas, relationships, DAX measures, CALCULATE, time intelligence and performance.

lessons.title: Star schema and relationships
lessons.summaryHtml:
A good Power BI model is usually a star schema: one fact table of events in the middle (Tickets), surrounded by dimension tables that describe them (Categories, Date). Relationships link the tables.

  • Cardinality says how rows match: one-to-many is the normal case, from dimension (one) to fact (many).
  • Cross-filter direction says which way filters flow. Single, from dimension to fact, is the safe default.
  • Only one relationship between two tables can be active. A Date table used for both CreatedDate and ClosedDate is a role-playing dimension; the second relationship stays inactive and is used with USERELATIONSHIP.

You also set table and column properties, create a common date table with DAX and mark it as a date table.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A data model is the set of tables Power BI holds, plus the relationships between them. The shape Microsoft recommends is the star schema. One table of events sits in the middle. Tables that describe those events sit around it, like the points of a star.

Think of a library. The loan records are the middle table: every time someone borrows a book, there is a new row. Around it sit a list of members, a list of books and a calendar. Each loan points to one member, one book and one date.

In the Help Desk, Tickets is the middle table. Categories and a Date table describe each ticket.

Why it matters

Relationships decide how filters travel. When a user clicks “Network” in a slicer, the relationship carries that filter from Categories to Tickets, and every visual updates. If the relationships are wrong, numbers are wrong, often without any error message.

A clean star schema also makes DAX simpler and reports faster. Many performance problems come from a messy model, not from slow formulas. The exam spends a lot of time on this topic because it underpins everything else.

How it works

1. Fact and dimension tables.

Fact tableDimension table
HoldsEvents or transactionsDescriptions of people, places, things, dates
RowsMany, and grows over timeFewer, one per item
ColumnsKeys and numbers (HoursToResolve)Key and text attributes (Name, Team)
Help DeskTicketsCategories, Date

If a dimension is split into further linked tables (for example Categories linked to a separate Teams table), you get a snowflake. Power BI works best when you flatten those into one dimension.

2. Cardinality.

CardinalityMeaningWhen
One-to-many (1:*)One dimension row matches many fact rowsThe normal case: Categories to Tickets
One-to-one (1:1)Each row matches exactly one rowRare; often a sign two tables should be combined
Many-to-many (*:*)Neither side has unique valuesSpecial cases, such as budgets stored at a different grain; use with care

The one side needs a column with unique values. If CategoryID repeated in Categories, a one-to-many relationship could not be created.

3. Cross-filter direction. Single means filters flow from the one side to the many side only. Both means they also flow back. Single is the recommended default. Both can cause ambiguous paths and slower queries, so use it only for a specific need.

4. Active and inactive relationships. Between two tables, only one relationship can be active. Others are inactive and shown as dashed lines. Visuals use the active one automatically. A measure can switch to an inactive one with USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.

5. Role-playing dimensions. Tickets has two dates: CreatedDate and ClosedDate. One Date table plays both roles. CreatedDate is active; ClosedDate is inactive. This is called a role-playing dimension. An alternative is to create two separate date tables, one per role.

6. A common date table. Time calculations need a proper date table: one row per day, no gaps, covering every date in your data. You can create it with DAX as a calculated table:

Date =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2026, 1, 1 ), DATE ( 2026, 12, 31 ) ),
    "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "MMM" ),
    "MonthNo", MONTH ( [Date] )
)

CALENDARAUTO() is an alternative that builds the range from the dates found in the model. Then use Mark as date table and choose the Date column.

7. Table and column properties. In Model view you can rename, hide key columns from report view, set formats, set a data category (such as City for maps), set Sort by column (Month sorted by MonthNo), choose a default summarization, and group fields into display folders.

8. Calculated columns and calculated tables. A calculated table is built with DAX, such as the Date table above. A calculated column adds a stored value per row. Use them when the value is needed for slicing, filtering or relationships and cannot easily be made in Power Query.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In Model view, check the relationship Categories[CategoryID] to Tickets[CategoryID]. It should be one-to-many with single direction. Categories is the one side because each CategoryID appears once there.
  2. Create the Date table with the DAX above and mark it as a date table.
  3. Drag Date[Date] to Tickets[CreatedDate]. Power BI creates an active one-to-many relationship.
  4. Drag Date[Date] to Tickets[ClosedDate]. It appears as a dashed inactive line, because an active path already exists.
  5. Set Date[Month] to sort by MonthNo, and hide Tickets[CategoryID], Tickets[CreatedDate] and Tickets[ClosedDate] from report view so authors use the Date table instead.
  6. A slicer on Categories[Team] now filters Tickets through the relationship. A visual by Date[Month] counts tickets by the month they were created. In lesson B.9 you will write a measure that uses the inactive ClosedDate relationship to count tickets by the month they were closed.
Watch out: tickets that are still open have an empty ClosedDate. That is fine: they simply do not match any date through the inactive relationship.

Common mistakes

  • Setting cross-filter direction to Both everywhere “just in case”.
  • Thinking two tables can have two active relationships at the same time.
  • Using the date columns in Tickets directly in visuals instead of a proper Date table.
  • Forgetting Sort by column, so months sort alphabetically.
  • Keeping a snowflake of small linked tables when one flat dimension would be simpler.

How the exam asks about it

  • “One date table, two date columns in the fact” points to an active plus an inactive relationship and USERELATIONSHIP, or to a role-playing dimension.
  • “Unique values on one side” points to one-to-many. “Neither side is unique” points to many-to-many.
  • “Months sort alphabetically” points to Sort by column.
  • “Time intelligence functions return wrong results” often points to a missing or unmarked date table.
  • “Filter must also flow from fact to dimension for this one scenario” points to Both direction, used sparingly.

Describes the facts, such as categories, dates or people, with one row per item.
How rows match across a relationship: one-to-many, one-to-one or many-to-many.
Which way a relationship passes filters: single or both.
One dimension, such as Date, related to a fact table in more than one way.

quiz.question: Tickets has CreatedDate and ClosedDate. You want one Date table to filter both, and slicers should use CreatedDate by default. What should you set up?
options: An active relationship on CreatedDate and an inactive one on ClosedDate
A second copy of the Date table only

quiz.question: The Month column in a visual sorts as Apr, Feb, Jan, Jun, Mar, May. How do you fix it?

One-to-many from Categories to Tickets, single direction
quiz.explanation: The dimension is the one side and the fact is the many side. Single direction from dimension to fact is the recommended default.

quiz.explanation: Bidirectional filters can create ambiguity and hurt performance. Use them only when a specific scenario needs them.

lessons.title: DAX fundamentals
lessons.summaryHtml:
DAX (Data Analysis Expressions) is the formula language of Power BI models. You use it to write measures, which are calculated at query time for whatever is filtered, and calculated columns, which are calculated row by row at refresh and stored in the model.

  • Filter context is the set of filters from slicers, visual rows and the filters pane that a measure sees.
  • Row context means “the current row”. Calculated columns have it; measures only get it inside iterators such as SUMX.
  • RELATED fetches a value from the one side of a relationship. DIVIDE divides safely and returns blank instead of an error when dividing by zero.

Prefer measures for totals and ratios. Use calculated columns only when you need a stored value per row, such as to slice or filter by it.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

DAX stands for Data Analysis Expressions. It is the formula language inside the Power BI model. It looks a little like Excel formulas, but it works on whole tables and columns, not on cells.

You write DAX in two main places. A measure is a calculation that answers a question for whatever the user is looking at, like “how many tickets?”. A calculated column adds a new value to every row of a table, like “which team owns this ticket?”.

A good picture is a calculator versus a sticker. A measure is a calculator you press each time the view changes. A calculated column is a sticker you put on every row once, at refresh, and it stays there.

Why it matters

Almost every number in a Power BI report comes from a measure. Managers ask for totals, averages, ratios and comparisons, and they want them to react to slicers. Only DAX measures do that properly.

Beginners often write the right formula in the wrong place. A ratio written as a calculated column gives wrong totals. A value needed in a slicer written as a measure cannot be placed in the slicer. Understanding the difference, and the two kinds of context, is the key to DAX.

How it works

1. Measures versus calculated columns.

MeasureCalculated column
When calculatedAt query time, every time a visual needs itAt refresh, once per row
Stored?No, only the formulaYes, uses memory in the model
Context it seesFilter context from the reportRow context of the current row
Reacts to slicers?YesNo, the value is fixed per row
Can go in a slicer or axis?NoYes
Help Desk exampleTotal Tickets, Close RateTeam from Categories

If you drag a numeric column into a visual, Power BI creates an implicit measure (such as Sum of HoursToResolve). Writing your own explicit measures is better: they have clear names, can be reused and are needed by some features.

2. Filter context. Filter context is the set of filters in force when a measure is evaluated. It comes from slicers, the rows and columns of a visual, the filters pane and cross-filtering from other visuals. In a matrix with Campus on rows, the North row has the filter Campus = North. The same measure gives a different result on each row because the filter context is different.

3. Row context. Row context means “I am looking at one specific row”. A calculated column has it automatically: when you write Tickets[HoursToResolve] * 2, DAX knows which row’s hours to use. A measure has no row context by default, so a bare column reference in a measure is an error. You must aggregate it, for example with SUM.

4. Aggregations and basic statistics.

FunctionReturns
COUNTROWS(table)Number of rows in a table
COUNT(column)Number of non-blank values in a column
DISTINCTCOUNT(column)Number of different values
SUM, AVERAGE, MIN, MAXTotal, mean, smallest, largest; blanks are ignored
MEDIAN, STDEV.PMiddle value and standard deviation

5. Iterators. Functions ending in X, such as SUMX, AVERAGEX and COUNTX, take a table and an expression. They create a row context, evaluate the expression for each row, then aggregate the results. Use them when you need a per-row calculation before adding up.

6. RELATED. RELATED follows a relationship from the many side to the one side and returns a value for the current row. It needs a row context, so you use it in calculated columns or inside an iterator. RELATEDTABLE goes the other way and returns the matching rows from the many side.

7. DIVIDE. DIVIDE(numerator, denominator) returns blank instead of an error when the denominator is zero or blank. You can pass a third argument as an alternate result. Use it for every ratio.

8. Quick measures. Power BI can generate common measures (such as running totals or averages per category) from a dialog. They write real DAX you can read and edit, which is a good way to learn patterns.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Create these measures on the Tickets table:

Total Tickets = COUNTROWS ( Tickets )
Avg Hours = AVERAGE ( Tickets[HoursToResolve] )
Agents Used = DISTINCTCOUNT ( Tickets[AssignedTo] )
Closed Tickets =
    COUNTROWS ( FILTER ( Tickets, Tickets[Status] = "Closed" ) )
Close Rate = DIVIDE ( [Closed Tickets], [Total Tickets] )

Avg Hours only averages closed tickets, because open tickets have blank HoursToResolve and AVERAGE ignores blanks. That is exactly what you want.

Now a weighted measure with an iterator. High priority tickets count double:

Weighted Hours =
SUMX (
    Tickets,
    IF ( Tickets[Priority] = "High",
         Tickets[HoursToResolve] * 2,
         Tickets[HoursToResolve] )
)

SUMX walks through each ticket in the current filter context, works out the weighted hours for that row, then adds them up.

Finally, a calculated column on Tickets:

Team = RELATED ( Categories[Team] )

Put Campus on the rows of a matrix with Total Tickets and Close Rate. Pick High in a Priority slicer. Every measure recalculates for the new filter context. The Team column does not change, because it was stored at refresh. You can, however, use Team in a slicer, which you could not do with a measure.

The DAX console in this lesson uses the same cleaned dataset. Change its Campus slicer and watch the same formula return different results.

Common mistakes

  • Writing ratios as calculated columns. The totals row then adds up percentages, which is meaningless.
  • Referencing a bare column in a measure, such as Tickets[HoursToResolve] * 2, without an aggregation or iterator.
  • Using RELATED in a measure without a row context, or in the wrong direction (from the one side).
  • Using the / operator for ratios and getting errors when a filter leaves no rows.
  • Creating many calculated columns “just in case”, which wastes memory.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Must respond to slicers” or “ratio” points to a measure. “Use as a slicer, axis or relationship key” points to a calculated column.
  • “Multiply per row, then total” points to an iterator such as SUMX.
  • “Bring a value from the related lookup table into each row” points to RELATED.
  • “Avoid divide-by-zero errors” points to DIVIDE.
  • “Count unique people or products” points to DISTINCTCOUNT, not COUNT.

lessons.title: CALCULATE and filter context
lessons.summaryHtml:
CALCULATE is the most important DAX function. It evaluates an expression in a modified filter context: it takes the filters coming from the report, then adds, replaces or removes filters according to its arguments.

  • A simple filter such as Tickets[Priority] = "High" replaces any existing filter on that column and keeps filters on other columns.
  • FILTER gives you row-by-row conditions; ALL removes filters, which is how you build “percent of total”.
  • KEEPFILTERS makes a filter intersect with the existing one instead of replacing it.
  • Inside a row context, CALCULATE performs context transition: the current row becomes a filter.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

In lesson B.7 you learned that every measure runs inside a filter context: the filters coming from slicers and visuals. CALCULATE lets a measure change that context before it calculates.

Think of a pair of glasses. The report hands the measure a pair of glasses that only shows North campus tickets. CALCULATE can swap one lens (“show High priority instead”), add a lens (“also only Closed”), or take the glasses off completely (“show everything”).

The basic shape is:

CALCULATE ( <expression>, <filter1>, <filter2>, ... )

The expression is usually a measure. The filters say how to change the context.

Why it matters

Most useful business questions are comparisons. “How many High priority tickets?” “What share of all tickets is this campus?” “How does this compare with last month?” Each one needs a number calculated under different filters from the ones on screen. CALCULATE is how you get it.

It is also the function beginners find hardest, because results depend on filters you cannot see in the formula. Once you understand the few rules below, most of DAX becomes predictable.

How it works

1. Start with the outer filter context. CALCULATE first takes all the filters the report applies: slicers, the current row of the visual and the filters pane.

2. Simple column filters replace. A filter such as Tickets[Priority] = "High" removes any existing filter on the Priority column and applies the new one. Filters on other columns, such as Campus, stay in place. Behind the scenes DAX treats it as a FILTER over ALL values of that column.

3. Several filter arguments combine with AND. CALCULATE([Total Tickets], Tickets[Priority] = "High", Tickets[Status] = "Closed") counts tickets that are High and Closed.

4. The main modifiers.

ModifierWhat it doesHelp Desk use
Column = valueReplaces the filter on that columnHigh priority tickets
FILTER(table, condition)Keeps rows that meet a row-by-row condition, including conditions using measures or several columnsTickets that took more than 8 hours
ALL(table or column)Removes filters from that table or columnDenominator for share of all tickets
REMOVEFILTERS(...)Same effect as ALL when used as a CALCULATE filter; clearer nameIgnore the Campus slicer
KEEPFILTERS(filter)Intersects with existing filters instead of replacing themHigh count only on the High row
USERELATIONSHIP(col1, col2)Uses an inactive relationship for this calculationCount tickets by closed date

5. FILTER, and where to point it. FILTER iterates a table row by row, so it can test any condition. Filtering a whole large table is slower than filtering a single column. When a simple column condition works, prefer it. Use FILTER when the condition is more complex, for example comparing a column to a number or combining columns with OR.

6. ALL for percent of total. ALL(Tickets) removes every filter on the Tickets table. ALL(Tickets[Campus]) removes only the Campus filter and keeps others, such as Priority. Choose the narrowest one that answers the question.

7. KEEPFILTERS, briefly. In a matrix with Priority on rows, CALCULATE([Total Tickets], Tickets[Priority] = "High") shows the High count on every row, because it replaces the row’s Priority filter. Wrapping the condition in KEEPFILTERS makes it intersect: the High row shows the High count and the Low and Medium rows show blank.

8. Context transition, at beginner level. When CALCULATE runs where there is a row context, such as in a calculated column or inside SUMX, it turns the current row into a filter. This is called context transition. Also, whenever you reference a measure inside a row context, DAX wraps it in CALCULATE for you, so context transition happens automatically.

Remember: a calculated column has row context but no filter context. Without CALCULATE, an aggregation in a calculated column sees the whole table.

Example: Campus Help Desk

Start from Total Tickets = COUNTROWS(Tickets) and add:

High Tickets =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Tickets], Tickets[Priority] = "High" )

Long Tickets =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Tickets],
        FILTER ( Tickets, Tickets[HoursToResolve] > 8 ) )

All Tickets =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Tickets], ALL ( Tickets ) )

Share of Total =
    DIVIDE ( [Total Tickets], [All Tickets] )

High Keep =
    CALCULATE ( [Total Tickets],
        KEEPFILTERS ( Tickets[Priority] = "High" ) )
  1. Select North in the Campus slicer. Total Tickets shows North tickets. High Tickets shows North High tickets, because the Campus filter stays and only Priority changes.
  2. All Tickets shows 60, the whole dataset, because ALL removed the Campus filter. Share of Total shows North’s share of all tickets.
  3. Change All Tickets to use ALL(Tickets[Campus]). Then add a Priority slicer set to High. The denominator now ignores Campus but still respects Priority, so you get North’s share of all High tickets.
  4. Build a matrix with Priority on rows. High Tickets repeats the same value on every row. High Keep shows a value only on the High row.
  5. Context transition: on the Categories table, add two calculated columns. 
    Rows Plain = COUNTROWS ( Tickets )
Rows Per Category = CALCULATE ( COUNTROWS ( Tickets ) )
    Rows Plain shows 60 on every category, because there is no filter context. Rows Per Category turns the current category row into a filter, which flows through the relationship to Tickets, so each row shows its own count.

Try the same formulas in the DAX console for this lesson and switch its Campus slicer to see the filter context change.

Common mistakes

  • Expecting a column filter in CALCULATE to add to the visual’s filter on the same column. It replaces it unless you use KEEPFILTERS.
  • Using ALL(Tickets) when only one column’s filter should be removed.
  • Filtering a whole table with FILTER when a simple column condition would do.
  • Forgetting that measures used inside a calculated column or iterator trigger context transition.
  • Thinking CALCULATE ignores slicers. It keeps every filter it does not explicitly change.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Percent of grand total” or “ignore the slicer for this measure” points to ALL or REMOVEFILTERS inside CALCULATE.
  • “Only for High priority, but still respect other slicers” points to a Boolean filter in CALCULATE.
  • “Should not override the filter already applied by the visual” points to KEEPFILTERS.
  • “Condition compares a column to a value or uses a measure” points to FILTER.
  • “Calculated column returns the same total on every row” points to missing CALCULATE and context transition.

CALCULATE turning the current row context into an equivalent filter context.

lessons.title: Time intelligence and advanced calculations
lessons.summaryHtml:
Time intelligence means comparing numbers across time: year-to-date, last month, same period last year. It needs a proper date table with one row per day, marked as the date table and related to your fact table. Functions such as TOTALYTD, DATESYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and DATEADD then shift the date filter for you inside CALCULATE.

  • USERELATIONSHIP turns on an inactive relationship (like Tickets[ClosedDate]) for one measure.
  • Semi-additive measures (balances, backlogs) must not be summed across time; take the closing value instead.
  • Shortcuts: statistical functions, quick measures, calculated tables, calculation groups and visual calculations.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Managers love questions about time. How many tickets so far this year? Is this month busier than last month? How many tickets did we close in March? Answering these by hand is slow. Time intelligence is a family of DAX functions that answer them for you.

Think of a wall calendar. You point at a month, and a helper instantly tells you the total “from January up to here” or “the same month last year”. The calendar is your date table. The helper is the time intelligence function. Without a proper calendar, the helper cannot count.

This lesson also covers other advanced tools you will meet on PL-300: inactive relationships, semi-additive measures, statistics, quick measures, calculated tables, calculation groups and visual calculations.

Why it matters

Almost every business report compares periods. Sales teams track year-to-date revenue. A help desk tracks tickets opened and closed per month. Finance tracks closing balances at month end. If each of these needed a custom formula full of date logic, reports would be slow to build and full of bugs.

A clean date table plus a few well-known functions makes these measures short and reliable. The exam tests this area heavily, because it combines modeling (the date table and relationships) with DAX (CALCULATE and filter context).

How it works

1. The date table. Time intelligence needs a table with one row per day. The date column must have unique values, no blanks and no gaps. It should cover whole years that include all your data. You can build it with DAX:

Date =
ADDCOLUMNS (
    CALENDAR ( DATE ( 2026, 1, 1 ), DATE ( 2026, 12, 31 ) ),
    "Year", YEAR ( [Date] ),
    "Month No", MONTH ( [Date] ),
    "Month", FORMAT ( [Date], "MMM" ),
    "Quarter", "Q" & QUARTER ( [Date] )
)

CALENDARAUTO() is an alternative. It scans the model’s date columns and builds whole years around them. After creating the table, choose Mark as date table and pick the Date column. Set Month to sort by Month No, or months will sort alphabetically. Once you have your own date table, turn off Auto date/time in the options, because it creates hidden date tables that waste memory.

2. Common time intelligence functions. Most of them return a set of dates. You use that set as a filter inside CALCULATE.

FunctionWhat it doesExample
TOTALYTDEvaluates an expression from the start of the year to the last date in contextTOTALYTD([Ticket Count], 'Date'[Date])
DATESYTDReturns the year-to-date dates; use inside CALCULATECALCULATE([Ticket Count], DATESYTD('Date'[Date]))
SAMEPERIODLASTYEARShifts the current dates back exactly one yearCALCULATE([Ticket Count], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date]))
DATEADDShifts dates by a number of days, months, quarters or yearsCALCULATE([Ticket Count], DATEADD('Date'[Date], -1, MONTH))

TOTALYTD and CALCULATE with DATESYTD give the same result. Both accept an optional year-end date for fiscal years, such as a year ending 31 March.

3. USERELATIONSHIP. Tickets has two dates: CreatedDate and ClosedDate. Only one relationship between Date and Tickets can be active. The ClosedDate one is inactive (a dashed line). This is a role-playing dimension: one Date table plays two roles. To count by closed date, activate it inside one measure:

Tickets closed =
CALCULATE (
    [Ticket Count],
    USERELATIONSHIP ( Tickets[ClosedDate], 'Date'[Date] )
)

4. Semi-additive measures. Some numbers can be added across products or campuses but not across time. A bank balance on 31 January plus the balance on 28 February is not a meaningful number. For these, you want the closing value of the period. A common pattern uses LASTNONBLANK:

Closing balance =
CALCULATE (
    SUM ( Balances[Amount] ),
    LASTNONBLANK ( 'Date'[Date], CALCULATE ( SUM ( Balances[Amount] ) ) )
)

LASTDATE and functions such as CLOSINGBALANCEMONTH follow the same idea. The open ticket backlog is also semi-additive, as the example shows.

5. Basic statistics. DAX has AVERAGE, MEDIAN, MIN, MAX, STDEV.P, STDEV.S, VAR.P and PERCENTILE.INC. The median is often better than the average for resolution times, because a few very long tickets pull the average up.

6. Quick measures. Right-click a table and choose New quick measure. Pick a calculation such as running total or year-to-date, drop in fields, and Power BI writes the DAX. Always read the generated code; it is a great way to learn.

7. Calculated tables. Created with New table and a DAX expression. Good uses: the date table, a summary table, or a copy of a dimension for a second role. They are computed at refresh and stored in the model.

8. Calculation groups. A calculation group holds reusable calculation items. Each item wraps whatever measure is in the visual using SELECTEDMEASURE(). One “Time” group with Current, YTD and Prior month items works for every measure. You create them in Model view (or with external tools). Creating one sets the model to discourage implicit measures, so you use explicit measures.

YTD = CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), DATESYTD ( 'Date'[Date] ) )
Prior month = CALCULATE ( SELECTEDMEASURE (), DATEADD ( 'Date'[Date], -1, MONTH ) )

9. Visual calculations. A newer feature. You select a visual and choose New calculation. The DAX runs on the data already in that visual, not on the whole model. Functions like RUNNINGSUM, MOVINGAVERAGE and PREVIOUS make running totals and period comparisons easy. The calculation lives in the visual only.

ToolStored whereBest for
MeasureModelReusable calculations in any visual
Calculated columnModel, one value per rowRow-level values you slice or filter by
Calculated tableModel, a new tableDate table, summary or role-playing copy
Calculation groupModelSame logic applied to many measures
Visual calculationOne visualRunning totals and comparisons within a visual

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create the Date table above, mark it, and relate Date[Date] to Tickets[CreatedDate] (active) and Tickets[ClosedDate] (inactive).
  2. Base measure: Ticket Count = COUNTROWS(Tickets).
  3. Year-to-date: Tickets YTD = TOTALYTD([Ticket Count], 'Date'[Date]). In a matrix by month, June shows every ticket created from January to June.
  4. Previous month: CALCULATE([Ticket Count], DATEADD('Date'[Date], -1, MONTH)). February shows January’s count.
  5. Same period last year returns blank. The data only covers 2026, so there is nothing to compare. That is correct, not a bug.
  6. Add Tickets closed with USERELATIONSHIP. Compare it with Ticket Count per month: tickets created in March may close in April.
  7. Open backlog is semi-additive. It is the number of tickets still open at the end of a period:
Open backlog =
VAR d = MAX ( 'Date'[Date] )
RETURN
    CALCULATE (
        [Ticket Count],
        REMOVEFILTERS ( 'Date' ),
        Tickets[CreatedDate] <= d,
        ISBLANK ( Tickets[ClosedDate] ) || Tickets[ClosedDate] > d
    )

By month, it shows the backlog on the last day of each month. The yearly total shows the backlog at year end, not the sum of six monthly figures.

Remember: time intelligence functions filter the date table. If the date column is not continuous, or the date table is not related to the fact table, results will be wrong or blank.

Common mistakes

  • Using Tickets[CreatedDate] directly in time intelligence instead of a proper date table.
  • Forgetting to mark the date table or to sort Month by Month No.
  • Making the ClosedDate relationship active and breaking every other measure. Keep one active and use USERELATIONSHIP.
  • Summing balances or backlogs across months. Semi-additive values need the closing value.
  • Thinking a visual calculation can be reused in other visuals. It lives in one visual only.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Two date columns in the fact table, report by the second one” → USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.
  • “Inventory, balance, headcount, total across time is wrong” → semi-additive measure with LASTNONBLANK or LASTDATE.
  • “Same logic for many measures, avoid duplicating measures” → calculation group with SELECTEDMEASURE.
  • “Time intelligence returns unexpected results” → check the date table: continuous, marked, related.

terms.definition: A table with one row per day and no gaps, marked as the model’s date table and used by time intelligence functions.
DAX functions that change the date filter, such as DATESYTD, SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR and DATEADD.
A CALCULATE modifier that activates an inactive relationship for that one calculation.
A measure that can be summed across some dimensions but not across time, such as a stock level or open backlog.
A set of reusable calculation items (like YTD or Prior month) that apply to any measure through SELECTEDMEASURE().

lessons.examTip: Two dates in one fact table and a question about “closed” or “shipped” counts? The answer is almost always USERELATIONSHIP inside CALCULATE.

quiz.question: A warehouse model stores stock on hand for every product every day. Users complain that the yearly total shows 365 days of stock added together. What kind of measure do you need?

quiz.question: You have 12 measures and each needs YTD, prior month and prior year versions. You want to avoid writing 36 new measures. What should you create?

lessons.title: Optimize model performance
lessons.summaryHtml:
A fast report starts with a small, clean model. Remove columns and rows you do not need, reduce granularity (for example keep dates, not date-times), and keep a star schema with single-direction relationships where possible.

To find what is slow, use Performance Analyzer: it records how long each visual takes and splits the time into the DAX query, the visual display and other work. Copy the slow query into DAX query view to test and rewrite it. Fix the biggest cost first, then measure again.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A slow report is like a heavy backpack. You can walk faster by carrying less, and by packing smarter. In Power BI, carrying less means loading fewer rows and columns. Packing smarter means a clean star schema and efficient DAX.

Optimizing is also about measuring. Before you change anything, you find out what is slow. Power BI Desktop gives you two tools for this: Performance Analyzer and DAX query view.

Why it matters

Users give up on slow reports. If a page takes a long time to load, people go back to spreadsheets. Large models also take longer to refresh and can hit the size limits of your licence or capacity. A smaller model is cheaper to run and easier to maintain.

Imagine the Help Desk data grows to years of tickets from many campuses. A model that felt instant with 60 rows can feel sluggish with millions. Good habits now save pain later.

How it works

1. How Import models store data. In Import mode, Power BI stores data in memory, column by column, and compresses each column. Columns with few distinct values (like Priority) compress very well. Columns with many distinct values (like a date-time to the second, or a long free-text description) compress poorly. So the number of distinct values, called cardinality, drives model size.

2. Remove what you do not need.

  • Columns: remove unused columns in Power Query. Hiding a column in the report does not remove it from memory.
  • Rows: filter out rows no one reports on, such as test tickets or years outside the reporting range.
  • Staging queries: turn off Enable load for helper queries that only feed other queries.
  • Auto date/time: turn it off when you have your own date table. It builds a hidden date table for every date column.

3. Reduce granularity. Granularity is the level of detail per row. If every report uses daily totals, you may not need one row per transaction. You can group rows in Power Query (for example, tickets per day per category) or split a date-time column into a date column, dropping the time. Fewer, coarser rows mean a smaller, faster model. The trade-off: you lose the detail, so only do this when the detail is truly not needed.

4. Model design.

  • Use a star schema: facts in the middle, dimensions around them.
  • Prefer one-to-many relationships with single-direction filtering. Bidirectional filters and many-to-many relationships cost more and can give confusing results.
  • Use measures instead of calculated columns when a value is only needed as an aggregate.
  • Use whole-number keys for relationships where you can.

5. Performance Analyzer. Open it from the ribbon, select Start recording, then interact with the report or choose Refresh visuals. Each visual gets a line with its total time, split into parts:

PartWhat it meansIf this is large
DAX queryTime for the model to answer the visual’s queryLook at the measures, relationships and model size
Visual displayTime for the visual to draw on screenToo many data points, heavy custom visuals, complex formatting
OtherTime waiting, for example behind other visualsToo many visuals on one page; consider fewer visuals

You can copy the DAX query of any visual, or send it to DAX query view.

6. DAX query view. This is a view in Power BI Desktop, next to Report, Table and Model views. You write queries that start with EVALUATE and see the result as a table. It is the place to test a measure, compare two versions, and check results quickly.

EVALUATE
SUMMARIZECOLUMNS (
    Categories[Name],
    "Tickets", [Ticket Count],
    "Median hours", [Median hours]
)

7. Efficient DAX habits.

  • Use variables (VAR) to calculate a value once and reuse it.
  • Use simple column filters in CALCULATE, like Tickets[Priority] = "High", rather than FILTER(Tickets, ...) over the whole table when a column filter is enough.
  • Use DIVIDE for safe division.
  • Avoid iterating huge tables with nested X functions when a plain aggregation works.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. On the Overview page, open Performance Analyzer, start recording and refresh visuals.
  2. Suppose the matrix of AssignedTo by Status is the slowest. Expand it: most time is in DAX query.
  3. Copy the query and open it in DAX query view. Run it to confirm it returns the same numbers.
  4. You look at the measure behind it. It filters with FILTER(Tickets, Tickets[Priority] = "High"). Rewrite it with the simple boolean filter Tickets[Priority] = "High" inside CALCULATE, run both versions, and check the results match.
  5. In Power Query, review the columns. If you had loaded a free-text description column that no visual uses, remove it.
  6. Turn off Auto date/time, because you already have a Date table.
  7. Record again and compare. With 60 rows the gain is tiny, but the same steps matter on large models.
Watch out: the first time a visual loads, results may not be cached; later runs can look faster. Refresh visuals several times and compare fairly before and after a change.

Common mistakes

  • Hiding columns and thinking the model is smaller. Only removing them in Power Query helps.
  • Turning on bidirectional filters “just in case”. They slow queries and can cause ambiguity.
  • Putting many visuals on one page. Each visual sends its own query.
  • Loading date-time to the second when reports only need the date.
  • Guessing the problem instead of measuring with Performance Analyzer.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Identify which visual is slow” or “measure load time per visual” → Performance Analyzer.
  • “Run and test a DAX query”, “EVALUATE” → DAX query view.
  • “Reduce model size”, “improve refresh time” → remove unused columns and rows, reduce granularity, lower cardinality.
  • “Visual display time is high” → too many data points or visuals, not the model.
