domains.name: Visualize and analyze
domains.blurb: Build reports, tell stories with bookmarks and drillthrough, and find trends with AI.

lessons.title: Build reports
lessons.summaryHtml:
A report is a set of pages with visuals built on your semantic model. Pick the visual that fits the question: bars to compare, lines for trends, cards for one key number, matrix for detail. Then format it, apply a theme for consistent colours, and add conditional formatting to highlight what matters.

  • Filter with slicers and the Filters pane (visual, page or all pages).
  • Copilot can create a report page, suggest content and write a narrative summary, when your workspace has the required paid capacity.
  • Use a paginated report, built in Power BI Report Builder, when the output must print or export page by page.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A report is what people actually see. It is a set of pages, and each page holds visuals: charts, cards, tables, maps and slicers. All of them read from the semantic model you built.

Building a report is like laying out a newspaper page. The headline number goes at the top. Supporting charts go below. Colours and fonts are consistent. Readers can find the story in a few seconds.

Why it matters

A correct model with a confusing report still fails. If the head of IT cannot see in ten seconds which campus has the most open high-priority tickets, the report has not done its job. PL-300 tests whether you can pick the right visual, format it, filter it, and choose the right kind of report for the need.

How it works

1. Choose the right visual. Start from the question, not the chart.

QuestionGood visualHelp Desk example
Compare categoriesBar or column chartTickets by category
Trend over timeLine chartTickets per month
One key numberCard or KPITotal open tickets
Part of a wholeStacked bar, donut or treemap (few parts)Share of tickets by priority
Detail by two dimensionsMatrixAgent by status
Row-level detailTableList of open tickets
Relationship between two numbersScatter chartTickets vs average hours per agent
LocationMap visualsTickets by site, if you have locations

2. Format visuals. The Format pane has settings for the visual itself (axes, data labels, colours) and general settings (title, border, shadow, alt text). Give every visual a clear title. Remove clutter such as gridlines you do not need.

3. Themes. A theme sets colours, fonts and default formatting for the whole report. Pick a built-in theme, customise the current theme, or import a JSON theme file. Organisations often share one theme so all reports look the same.

4. Conditional formatting. Colours that change with the data. In tables and matrices you can set background colour, font colour, data bars, icons and web URLs. The colour can come from a gradient, from rules (for example, above 10 is red), or from a field value. Many charts also support conditional colours.

5. Slicing and filtering.

  • Slicers sit on the canvas. Users click them to filter the page.
  • The Filters pane has three levels: this visual, this page, and all pages. Filters can be basic, advanced, Top N or relative date.
  • You can lock or hide filters so users cannot change or see them.

6. Configure the page. In the Format pane for the page, set canvas size (16:9, 4:3, letter or custom), background, wallpaper and page information.

7. Copilot in reports. When the workspace is on a paid capacity with Copilot enabled, Copilot can suggest content for a page, create a report page from a prompt, and write a summary in a narrative visual. Always check what Copilot produces: it only works as well as your model and field names.

8. Paginated reports. Normal Power BI reports are interactive and fit on a screen. Paginated reports are built with Power BI Report Builder. They are pixel-perfect and designed to print or export across many pages, like invoices, statements or long lists.

Power BI reportPaginated report
Built inPower BI Desktop or the servicePower BI Report Builder
Best forInteractive explorationPrinting, exporting, fixed layout
LengthFits the page canvasGrows across as many pages as needed

9. Visual calculations. From B.9: select a visual and add a New calculation for running totals or comparisons that only this visual needs.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Create an Overview page. Put a card with Ticket Count at the top left.
  2. Add a clustered bar chart of Ticket Count by Categories[Name]. Sort it descending.
  3. Add a line chart of Ticket Count by Date[Month]. Check Month sorts January to June.
  4. Add slicers for Campus and Priority. Because you cleaned the Campus values, the slicer shows exactly North, South and City.
  5. Add a matrix with AssignedTo on rows, Status on columns, Ticket Count as values. Apply a background colour gradient so heavy workloads stand out.
  6. Apply a theme and set a consistent title style.
  7. If Copilot is available, ask it to summarise the page in a narrative visual. Read the text and check each claim against the visuals.
Remember: dashboards and reports are different. A report has pages and lives in Desktop and the service. A dashboard is a single canvas of pinned tiles and exists only in the Power BI service.

Common mistakes

  • Using a pie or donut chart with many slices. Bars compare better.
  • Formatting every visual by hand instead of using a theme.
  • Choosing a normal report when the need is a printable, multi-page document.
  • Forgetting that a page-level filter affects all visuals on the page, not the whole report.
  • Trusting Copilot output without checking it against the data.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Print”, “pixel-perfect”, “invoice”, “many pages” → paginated report with Power BI Report Builder.
  • “Highlight values above a target in a table” → conditional formatting.
  • “Filter every page without a visible slicer” → Filters pane, all pages.
  • “Consistent colours across reports” → theme (JSON).

lessons.title: Storytelling and usability
lessons.summaryHtml:
A good report guides the reader. Bookmarks save a view (filters, visibility, page) and buttons can jump to them. Drillthrough takes a user from a summary to a detail page for one item. Custom tooltips show a small report page on hover.

  • Control how visuals affect each other with Edit interactions, and keep slicers aligned across pages with Sync slicers.
  • Use the Selection pane to group, layer, hide visuals and set tab order.
  • Design a mobile layout, set export options, allow personalization, check accessibility, and use automatic page refresh for DirectQuery data that changes often.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A report with good visuals still needs a guide. Storytelling features lead the reader: “start here, then look at this, then click for details”. Usability features make the report easy for everyone to use, on any screen.

Think of a museum. Signs guide you from room to room (navigation and bookmarks). A small card next to each painting tells you more (tooltips). A door marked “more about this artist” takes you to a detail room (drillthrough).

Why it matters

Different people want different depth. The head of IT wants the summary. A team lead wants to click into one category. An agent on a phone wants one number. Good design serves all three without building three reports.

The exam covers a long list of these features. The trick is to link each feature to the problem it solves.

How it works

1. Bookmarks. A bookmark captures the state of a page: filters, slicers, sort order, drill level and which visuals are visible. You create them in the Bookmarks pane. Each bookmark can choose to capture data, display and current page. Link a button to a bookmark to switch views, such as “Chart view” and “Table view”, on one page.

2. Navigation. Buttons can navigate to a page or a bookmark. The page navigator and bookmark navigator add a set of buttons automatically.

3. Custom tooltips. Create a small page, turn on Allow use as tooltip, and set the canvas size to Tooltip. Then, on a visual’s tooltip settings, choose that report page. Hovering over a bar now shows a mini report filtered to that bar.

4. Interactions between visuals. By default, clicking one visual cross-filters or cross-highlights others. Use Edit interactions to choose Filter, Highlight or None for each pair of visuals.

5. Sorting. Sort a visual by any field in it. For text that has a natural order, like month names, use Sort by column on the model so Jan comes before Feb.

6. Sync slicers. The Sync slicers pane lets one slicer filter several pages. For each page, choose whether the slicer is synced and whether it is visible.

7. Selection pane. Lists every object on the page. Use it to hide or show objects, change layer order (which is in front), group objects, and set the tab order for keyboard users.

8. Drillthrough. Put a field, such as Category Name, in the Drillthrough well of a detail page. Users right-click a data point on another page and choose Drill through. The detail page opens filtered to that item, with a back button.

9. Export settings. In report settings you choose what users may export from visuals: summarized data, underlying data, or nothing. Admins can also restrict export at tenant level.

10. Mobile layout. Use the mobile layout view to place visuals for a phone screen. The desktop layout is unchanged.

11. Personalization. When Personalize visuals is on, report readers in the service can change a visual’s type or fields for themselves, without editing the report. They can save their view as a personal bookmark.

12. Accessibility. Add alt text to visuals. Set a logical tab order. Use enough colour contrast and do not rely on colour alone; add labels or markers. Give every visual a clear title.

13. Automatic page refresh. For DirectQuery sources, a page can refresh on a fixed interval or when a change is detected. Admins can set the minimum allowed interval. It is not for Import data, which uses scheduled refresh.

NeedFeature
Switch between views on one pageBookmarks and buttons
Details for one selected item on another pageDrillthrough
Extra detail on hoverReport page tooltip
Stop one visual filtering anotherEdit interactions
Same slicer on many pagesSync slicers
Readers change a visual for themselvesPersonalize visuals
Near real-time on DirectQueryAutomatic page refresh

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. Drillthrough: create a page “Category details” with Categories[Name] in the Drillthrough well. Add a table of TicketID, Priority, Status and AssignedTo. From the Overview bar chart, right-click Network and drill through.
  2. Tooltip: make a tooltip page with a card for Median hours and a small bar chart by Priority. Set it as the tooltip for the category bar chart. Hovering over Hardware now shows its median resolution time.
  3. Interactions: clicking a category highlights the line chart. The manager wants it filtered, so set the interaction to Filter.
  4. Sync slicers: sync the Campus slicer across Overview and Category details, visible only on Overview.
  5. Bookmarks: on Overview, create “Summary” (matrix hidden) and “Detail” (matrix visible). Add two buttons and group them in the Selection pane.
  6. Accessibility: add alt text such as “Bar chart of tickets by category” and check the tab order.
  7. Mobile: in mobile layout, place the Ticket Count card and the category chart.
Watch out: a bookmark captures data state by default. If you only want it to show or hide visuals, turn off Data for that bookmark, or it will also reset the user’s slicers.

Common mistakes

  • Using bookmarks when drillthrough is needed. Bookmarks do not pass the clicked item as a filter.
  • Forgetting to set the tooltip page canvas and Allow use as tooltip.
  • Expecting automatic page refresh to work on Import data.
  • Sorting month names alphabetically instead of using Sort by column.
  • Relying on red and green alone to show good and bad.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Right-click a value to see details on another page” → drillthrough.
  • “Toggle between chart and table on the same page” → bookmarks with buttons.
  • “Hover to see more information” → report page tooltip.
  • “Clicking one visual should not affect another” → Edit interactions, None.
  • “Screen reader”, “keyboard users” → alt text and tab order in the Selection pane.

lessons.title: Find patterns and trends
lessons.summaryHtml:
Power BI can do more than show numbers. It can help you find what the numbers are hiding. The Analyze feature explains why a value went up or down. Groups and bins put many values into a few buckets. Clustering finds natural groups of points on a scatter chart.

  • The Analytics pane adds reference lines, error bars and forecasts to supported visuals.
  • AI visuals such as Key influencers, Decomposition tree and Q&A answer “why” and “where” questions.
  • Anomaly detection on line charts flags unexpected points, and Copilot can summarize a semantic model in plain language.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

A report shows what happened. This lesson is about asking why it happened and what comes next. Power BI has built-in tools that do some of the detective work for you.

Think of a doctor reading a chart of your temperature. A plain chart shows the numbers. A good doctor also draws a normal line, spots the one strange reading, and guesses where the fever is heading. The tools in this lesson do the same for your data: reference lines, outlier spotting and forecasts.

Some tools are simple, such as grouping values into buckets. Others use machine learning, such as the Key influencers visual. You do not need to write any AI code. You drag fields into a visual and Power BI does the analysis.

Why it matters

Managers rarely ask “how many tickets did we get?”. They ask “why did tickets jump in March?”, “what makes a ticket take so long?” and “how busy will we be next month?”. Answering those by hand means building many charts and comparing them.

The pattern tools save that time. They also help people who are not analysts. A campus manager can right-click a point and get an explanation without asking the data team.

On PL-300, this is the “Identify patterns and trends” part of the Visualize and analyze area. Questions describe a business need and ask which feature fits it.

How it works

1. Analyze (explain the increase or decrease). In a chart, right-click a data point and choose Analyze. Power BI compares that point with the one before it. It then looks at other fields in the model and shows which ones contributed most to the change. It works best on simple additive measures such as counts and sums.

2. Grouping and binning. A group combines chosen values into one label, for example North and South into “Main campuses”. A bin splits a number or date column into equal-size buckets, for example HoursToResolve in steps of 4. Both are created from the field’s right-click menu with New group. They add a new column you can use on an axis or in a legend.

3. Clustering. On a scatter chart, Power BI can find clusters automatically. It groups points that sit close together into a new field. For example, agents with many tickets and low hours may form one cluster, and agents with few tickets and high hours another. Use it to discover segments you did not know existed.

4. The Analytics pane. When a supported visual is selected, the Analytics pane (the magnifying glass icon) lets you add extra lines. What appears depends on the visual type.

OptionWhat it showsHelp Desk use
Constant lineA fixed target valueA target of average hours to resolve
Average, median, min, max, percentile linesA line calculated from the data in the visualIs this month above the average month?
Trend lineThe overall direction of the dataAre tickets rising over the half year?
Error barsA range around each point, from upper and lower bound fields or measuresShow the lowest and highest hours per Campus
ForecastPredicted future values with a confidence band, on line charts with a continuous date axisExpected tickets for the next months

5. Outliers and anomalies. An outlier is a point far from the rest, which you often see on a scatter chart. Anomaly detection is a feature of line charts with a date axis. You turn on Find anomalies and Power BI marks points outside the expected range. Selecting a marked point shows possible explanations.

6. AI visuals.

VisualQuestion it answersClue words
Key influencersWhich factors most affect an outcome, and which segments stand out“what drives”, “what influences”, “more likely”
Decomposition treeHow a measure breaks down across dimensions, level by level“drill down”, “root cause”, “break down”
Q&AAnswers a question typed in natural language with a visual“ask in plain English”
Narrative visual (Copilot) or smart narrativeWrites a text summary of the page or visuals“text summary”, “written insights”

The Decomposition tree has AI splits. Instead of choosing the next field yourself, you ask for the high value or low value split, and Power BI picks the field that leads there.

7. Copilot and the semantic model. With Copilot available, you can ask it to summarize the semantic model or answer questions about the data in plain language. Copilot needs a paid capacity and must be enabled by the admin. Always check its answers against the report.

Remember: Key influencers tells you which factors matter. The Decomposition tree lets you follow a path through the numbers. Analyze explains one change between two points.

Example: Campus Help Desk

The Help Desk manager notices more closed tickets in March and wants to understand the workload.

  1. On a column chart of [Ticket Count] by Date[Month], she right-clicks March and chooses Analyze. Power BI shows that most of the increase came from one Campus and the Network category.
  2. She bins HoursToResolve with a bin size of 4. A column chart shows how resolution times spread out: many tickets close within a day, with a long tail of slow ones.
  3. She adds a Key influencers visual. Analyze is Priority, and Explain by is Campus, Name and AssignedTo. For Priority = High, it shows which category and campus make High more likely.
  4. She adds a Decomposition tree with [Total Hours]. She splits by Campus, then uses the high-value AI split, which picks the category that adds the most hours.
  5. On a line chart of tickets by date, she adds an Average line from the Analytics pane and a Forecast. She turns on Find anomalies and checks one flagged day.

The dataset is small (60 tickets), so AI results are only a demonstration. Real conclusions need more data.

Common mistakes

  • Thinking Key influencers and the Decomposition tree do the same job. One ranks factors; the other drills through levels.
  • Expecting forecasts on any visual. Forecasting needs a line chart with a continuous date axis.
  • Confusing a group (hand-picked values under one label) with a bin (equal-size numeric or date buckets).
  • Trusting AI results from very small datasets. Few rows can give misleading patterns.
  • Assuming Copilot works everywhere. It needs a suitable paid capacity and admin settings.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Why did the value change between two months?” → Analyze, explain the increase or decrease.
  • “Which factors make an outcome more likely?” → Key influencers. “Drill into the cause across several dimensions” → Decomposition tree.
  • “Predict future values” or “show a target line” → the Analytics pane: Forecast or a constant line.
  • “Group ages or amounts into ranges” → bins. “Find unexpected spikes” → anomaly detection on a line chart.

terms.definition: A bucket of equal size that groups numeric or date values, for example HoursToResolve in steps of 4.
An AI visual that ranks the factors that most affect a result, such as a ticket being High priority.
An AI visual that splits a measure step by step across dimensions so you can drill into the cause.
The pane that adds reference lines, error bars, trend lines and forecasts to supported visuals.
A data point outside the range the model expected, flagged by anomaly detection on a line chart.

lessons.examTip: Match the question word to the tool: “why did it change” → Analyze; “what drives it” → Key influencers; “break it down” → Decomposition tree; “future values” → Forecast.

steps: Download measures.txt and analysis-worksheet.md. Create Total Hours and Average Hours (and Ticket Count if missing) from measures.txt.
On a new page, add a column chart of [Ticket Count] by Campus. Right-click the tallest column and choose Analyze, then Explain the increase or a similar option if shown.
In the Data pane, right-click HoursToResolve and choose New group. Create bins of size 4. Build a column chart of Ticket Count by the new bin column.
Add a line chart with Date[Month] on the X-axis and [Ticket Count] on the Y-axis. In the Analytics pane, add an Average line and a Forecast if the option is available for your axis.
Add a Key influencers visual. Put Priority in Analyze and Campus, Categories[Name] and AssignedTo in Explain by. Choose High as the value to explain and read the result.
Add a Decomposition tree with [Total Hours] in Analyze and Campus, Name and AssignedTo in Explain by. Expand the tree and use the high-value AI split once.
Build a scatter chart of AssignedTo (Values), [Ticket Count] (X) and [Average Hours] (Y). Try the automatic clusters option from the visual’s More options menu if it appears.
Fill in every answer in analysis-worksheet.md, including the one-sentence finding.
check: The Campus column chart reads South 25, North 21, City 14.
In the bins chart the tallest bin is 12 (12 to under 16 hours) with 11 tickets, then 8 with 10; 14 tickets fall in (Blank) because they are not closed.
The Average line on the monthly chart sits at 10, and every month equals it.

quiz.question: The Help Desk manager sees that closed tickets jumped in March and asks which Campus or Category caused the increase. What is the quickest way to answer?
options: Right-click the March data point and use Analyze to explain the increase
Create a calculated table that copies March rows
Add an error bar to the chart
Create a new workspace for March
quiz.explanation: Analyze (explain the increase or decrease) compares the selected point with the previous one and shows which fields contributed most.

quiz.question: You want to show how many tickets took 0–4, 4–8 and 8–12 hours to resolve. HoursToResolve is a decimal column. What should you create?
quiz.explanation: Binning turns a continuous numeric or date column into equal-size buckets you can use on an axis.

quiz.question: A team lead asks: “Which factors make a ticket more likely to be High priority?” Which visual answers this directly?
quiz.explanation: Key influencers ranks the factors that most change the likelihood of a chosen outcome, such as Priority = High.

quiz.question: You want a line chart of monthly tickets to project the next three months with a confidence band. What should you use?
options: The Forecast option in the Analytics pane
quiz.explanation: Forecasting is added from the Analytics pane on supported line charts with a continuous date axis. It shows predicted values and a confidence interval.

lessons.title: Workspaces, sharing and refresh
lessons.summaryHtml:
Reports you build in Desktop become useful when you publish them to the Power BI service. There they live in a workspace, a shared space where a team builds and manages content. You then distribute content through an app, direct sharing, or embedding in places like Teams.

  • Dashboards are single pages of pinned tiles, built only in the service. Tiles can have data alerts, and reports and dashboards can have subscriptions.
  • Endorsement (promoted or certified) tells people which content to trust.
  • Scheduled refresh keeps Import models current. An on-premises data gateway is needed when the source sits on a local network or computer.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Power BI Desktop is where you build. The Power BI service is where people use what you built. Moving a report from Desktop to the service is called publishing.

Think of a restaurant. The workspace is the kitchen: the team cooks, tastes and fixes dishes there. The app is the dining room: guests only see finished plates. Refresh is restocking the kitchen with fresh ingredients. The gateway is the delivery van that brings ingredients from a farm the cloud cannot reach by itself.

This lesson covers all of these: workspaces, apps, dashboards, subscriptions and alerts, endorsement, gateways and scheduled refresh.

Why it matters

A report on your laptop helps only you. The Help Desk manager, campus leads and IT staff need the same numbers, updated every day, without asking you to send files. The service solves this with shared workspaces, controlled distribution and automatic refresh.

Governance matters too. When many people publish reports, users need to know which one is the official source. Endorsement solves that. On PL-300, this area is “Manage and secure Power BI”.

How it works

1. Workspaces. A workspace holds semantic models, reports, dashboards and other items. Everyone has My workspace for personal work, but team content belongs in a shared workspace. In the workspace settings you can set a name, description, contact list and, where available, a license mode or capacity. Working with others in shared workspaces generally needs Pro or Premium Per User licences, or a workspace on a capacity. A free trial is often available.

2. Publish, import and update. From Desktop, Publish sends the report and its semantic model to a workspace. Publishing again with the same name replaces them. You can also upload a .pbix file into a workspace from the service. After publishing, the report and semantic model are separate items, and other reports can connect to the same semantic model.

3. Dashboards. A dashboard is a single page of tiles. You pin visuals from one or more reports onto it. Dashboards exist only in the service; you cannot build them in Desktop. Tiles link back to their report.

4. Distribution methods.

MethodBest forNote
Workspace accessPeople who build and edit contentGive a workspace role (covered in B.15)
AppMany consumers who need a stable, read-only packageOne app per workspace; you choose audiences and update the app when ready
Direct sharingGiving one report or dashboard to a few peopleQuick, but harder to manage at scale
Embed in Teams or SharePointShowing reports where people already workViewers still need permission and a suitable licence
Publish to webTruly public data onlyAnyone with the link can see it, with no sign-in. Never use it for internal data

5. Apps. You create an app from a workspace, choose which items to include, and add one or more audiences. Each audience can see different content. When you change a report in the workspace, app users do not see it until you choose Update app.

6. Subscriptions and data alerts. A subscription emails a snapshot of a report page or dashboard on a schedule. A data alert is set on a dashboard tile, such as a card, KPI or gauge. It notifies you when the value goes above or below a threshold. Alerts can also start a Power Automate flow.

7. Endorsement. Promoted means the owner thinks the content is ready to use; content owners can set it. Certified means it meets the organisation’s quality standard; only people authorised by the Power BI admin can certify.

8. Gateways and scheduled refresh. An Import model holds a copy of the data. To keep it current, you configure scheduled refresh in the semantic model settings. You also provide data source credentials. The cloud service can reach cloud sources directly. It cannot reach a file on your laptop or a database on a local server. For those, you install an on-premises data gateway.

SourceGateway needed for refresh?
CSV on a local PC or network shareYes
SQL Server in the college’s own server roomYes (also for DirectQuery)
File in SharePoint Online or OneDrive for work or schoolNo
Azure SQL Database or other cloud sourcesUsually no

A gateway can run in standard mode, shared by many users and managed centrally, or personal mode, for one user only. Refresh frequency limits depend on your licence, so check the current documentation rather than guessing.

Watch out: DirectQuery and Direct Lake models do not need a scheduled import refresh in the same way, but DirectQuery to an on-premises source still needs a gateway.

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. You create a workspace called Help Desk Analytics and add the data team.
  2. From Desktop you publish the Help Desk report. The service now shows a report and a semantic model.
  3. Your model reads tickets.csv from a folder on your PC. To refresh every morning, you either install a gateway or move the file to SharePoint Online and change the data source. Moving it removes the need for a gateway.
  4. You pin the Open tickets card and the Campus chart to a dashboard called Help Desk Overview. On the card, you set an alert for when open tickets exceed a threshold.
  5. The manager subscribes to the report page and gets a snapshot by email each Monday.
  6. You publish an app for campus leads. Later you fix a chart and choose Update app so they see the fix.
  7. After review, the data lead certifies the semantic model so other report builders reuse it.

Common mistakes

  • Building dashboards in Desktop. Dashboards are made only in the service.
  • Thinking every refresh needs a gateway. Cloud sources usually do not.
  • Sharing from My workspace for team content. Use a shared workspace and an app.
  • Expecting app users to see changes immediately. You must update the app.
  • Using Publish to web for internal reports. It makes data public.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Data on a local server” or “on-premises” with refresh or DirectQuery → on-premises data gateway.
  • “Many users, read-only, control when changes appear” → an app with audiences.
  • “Notify when a value exceeds a threshold” → data alert on a dashboard tile. “Email a snapshot on a schedule” → subscription.
  • “Official, trusted content” → certify. “Highlight as ready without formal review” → promote.

terms.definition: A shared container in the Power BI service for semantic models, reports, dashboards and other items.
A packaged, read-only view of workspace content that you publish to chosen audiences and update when ready.
Software that securely connects the cloud service to data on a local network or computer, used for refresh and DirectQuery.
Labelling content as Promoted or Certified so people can find trusted items.
A notification when a dashboard tile value crosses a threshold you set.

lessons.examTip: Clue “source is on a local server or PC” → gateway. Clue “source is a cloud service like SharePoint Online or Azure SQL Database” → usually no gateway.

steps: Download publishing-checklist.md. In Power BI Desktop add the Open Tickets measure from it, put it in a card on Overview, and save.
In app.powerbi.com, create a workspace named Help Desk Analytics. A free trial may be offered if your licence cannot use shared workspaces.
In Power BI Desktop, choose Publish and select the Help Desk Analytics workspace. Open the report in the service when it finishes.

Pin the Ticket Count card, the Open Tickets card and the Campus chart to a new dashboard named Help Desk Overview. On the Open Tickets tile, set a data alert above a threshold higher than today’s value.
Open the semantic model settings. Look at Data source credentials, Gateway connection and Scheduled refresh, and fill in the Refresh plan table in the checklist.
On the report, create a subscription that emails you a snapshot of the Overview page.
In the workspace, create an app. Include the report and dashboard, add an audience, and publish it. Change the report in Desktop, republish, then choose Update app and see the change appear.
Open the semantic model settings and set Endorsement to Promoted.
check: The workspace lists a report and a semantic model, both named HelpDesk, plus the Help Desk Overview dashboard.
The dashboard tiles show Ticket Count 60 and Open Tickets 10.
The semantic model settings say scheduled refresh needs a gateway for the local CSV files, so the scheduled refresh cannot be turned on until a gateway (or a OneDrive/SharePoint source) is set up.
The app shows the report and dashboard, and after Update app it shows your change.

quiz.question: Your Help Desk semantic model imports tickets.csv from a folder on the IT office PC. The manager wants it refreshed every morning in the service. What is required?
quiz.explanation: Data on a local computer or network is not reachable by the cloud. An on-premises data gateway is required for scheduled refresh.

quiz.question: Fifty campus staff need a stable, read-only set of Help Desk reports. You want to keep working on changes without them seeing half-finished work. What should you use?
options: Give everyone the Member role in the workspace
Publish an app from the workspace and update it when changes are ready
quiz.explanation: An app separates what consumers see from work in progress. Changes appear for users only after you update the app.

quiz.question: The service desk lead wants an email when the Open Tickets card on a dashboard goes above 20. What should you set up?
options: A data alert on the dashboard tile
quiz.explanation: Data alerts are set on dashboard tiles such as cards, KPIs and gauges. They notify you when a value crosses a threshold.

quiz.question: The data team has reviewed the Help Desk semantic model and wants it marked as the official, trusted source across the organisation. What should they apply?
quiz.explanation: Certification is the higher endorsement level, applied by people the admin authorises. Promoted can be set by content owners without review.

lessons.title: Security and governance
lessons.summaryHtml:
Power BI security works in layers. Workspace roles (Admin, Member, Contributor, Viewer) decide what people can do in a workspace. Item-level access gives someone a single report, app or semantic model without the whole workspace. Row-level security (RLS) decides which rows of data a viewer can see.

  • Static RLS uses a fixed filter per role, such as one role per Campus.
  • Dynamic RLS uses USERPRINCIPALNAME() and a mapping table, so one role works for everyone.
  • You create roles in Desktop, test them with View as, and add users or groups to roles in the service.
  • Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview mark how confidential content is, and the label can follow data when it is exported.
lessons.contentHtml:
In plain words

Security in Power BI answers three questions. Who can get into this space? Who can open this item? Which rows can this person see? Each question has its own tool.

Think of a college library. The building card lets you into the library: that is the workspace role. A reading-room pass lets you into one room: that is item-level access. Inside the room, some shelves are locked unless your card matches: that is row-level security. A red “Confidential” sticker on a folder is a sensitivity label.

Why it matters

The Help Desk report has tickets from three campuses. The North lead should not see South’s tickets, and an agent may only need their own. Making one report per campus is slow to maintain and easy to get wrong. RLS lets one report and one semantic model serve everyone safely.

Labels matter too. Ticket data may include staff names. If someone exports it to Excel, the file should still be marked and protected. On PL-300, “Secure and govern Power BI items” covers all of this.

How it works

1. Workspace roles.

RoleCan doLimited by RLS?
AdminEverything, including managing access and deleting the workspaceNo
MemberCreate and edit content, add people with lower roles, publish and update the appNo
ContributorCreate, edit and delete contentNo
ViewerView and interact with content, not edit itYes

This is a key rule: RLS restricts only people with read access, such as Viewers, app users and people a report was shared with. Anyone who can edit the semantic model can see all its data.

2. Item-level access. You do not always need to give a workspace role. You can share one report or dashboard, include items in an app audience, or grant permissions on a semantic model. Semantic model permissions include Read (view reports on it), Build (create new reports on it) and Reshare. Build is what a report builder in another workspace needs to reuse your model.

3. Static RLS. You create roles in Desktop, under Modeling, Manage roles. Each role has a DAX filter on a table. The filter must return TRUE for rows the role can see. One role per Campus looks like this:

Role North:  [Campus] = "North"     (on Tickets)
Role South:  [Campus] = "South"
Role City:   [Campus] = "City"

Filters flow through relationships. A filter on the Categories table, such as [Team] = "Identity", also limits Tickets, because Categories filters Tickets. Static RLS is simple, but you need a new role for every new value.

4. Dynamic RLS. Here one role works for everyone. It uses USERPRINCIPALNAME(), which returns the signed-in user’s sign-in name, usually their email. You add a mapping table that links each email to the data they may see.

Staff table:  AssignedTo | Email
              Anu        | anu@college.edu
              Rahul      | rahul@college.edu

Relationship: Staff[AssignedTo] 1 → * Tickets[AssignedTo]

Role Own Tickets, filter on Staff:
[Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME()

When Anu signs in, the filter keeps only her Staff row. The relationship then keeps only her tickets. To give each Campus lead their Campus, use a mapping table of Email and Campus related to the Campus values instead.

5. Test with View as. In Desktop, choose View as under Modeling. Tick one or more roles to preview the report as that role. For dynamic RLS, also tick Other user and type an email, so USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns that value. Without this, Desktop shows all data to you as the author.

6. Assign members in the service. After publishing, open the semantic model’s Security page. Pick a role and add users or, better, security groups or Microsoft 365 groups. Groups mean you manage membership in Entra ID instead of editing roles. The service also has Test as role. Important: if a Viewer is in no role at all while RLS roles exist, they see no data.

7. Sensitivity labels. Labels such as Public, General or Confidential come from Microsoft Purview Information Protection and are set up by your organisation. You apply them in Desktop or the service. When data is exported to Excel, PowerPoint or PDF, supported exports carry the label and its protection. Labels can also pass to downstream content built from a labelled item. A label classifies and protects; it does not filter rows.

NeedTool
Let a team edit reportsWorkspace role (Member or Contributor)
Let someone view one report onlyShare the item or add them to an app audience
Let another team build reports on your modelBuild permission on the semantic model
Show each person only some rowsRLS (static or dynamic)
Mark and protect confidential contentSensitivity label

Example: Campus Help Desk

  1. In Desktop, you create roles North, South and City with filters on Tickets[Campus].
  2. You use View as with North and confirm only North tickets appear on every page.
  3. You add a Staff table with AssignedTo and Email, relate it to Tickets, and create the Own Tickets role with [Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME().
  4. With View as, you tick Own Tickets and Other user, and type Anu’s email. Only Anu’s tickets appear.
  5. You publish. On the semantic model’s Security page, you add the North Leads security group to North, and the Help Desk Agents group to Own Tickets.
  6. Campus leads get the Viewer role or app access, so RLS applies. The data team keeps Member access to edit.
  7. You apply the Confidential label, so exports to Excel stay marked.

Common mistakes

  • Giving a campus lead the Member or Contributor role and expecting RLS to limit them. It will not.
  • Assigning role members in Desktop. Roles are defined in Desktop; members are added in the service.
  • Using page or report filters for security. Users can change them. RLS is enforced in the model.
  • Forgetting to test dynamic RLS with a specific user in View as.
  • Thinking a sensitivity label hides data. It classifies and protects files; RLS filters rows.

How the exam asks about it

  • “Few fixed groups, such as regions” → static RLS roles. “Each user sees their own data” or “many users” → dynamic RLS with USERPRINCIPALNAME().
  • “Verify the role before publishing” → View as in Desktop. “Add users to a role” → the semantic model’s Security page in the service, ideally with groups.
  • “User still sees all data” → check their workspace role; editors bypass RLS.
  • “Build reports from our model without workspace access” → Build permission. “Classify and protect exported data” → sensitivity label.

terms.definition: Rules in the semantic model that filter which rows a user can see, defined as roles with DAX filters.
A DAX function that returns the signed-in user’s sign-in name, usually their email address, used for dynamic RLS.
A Desktop feature that shows the report as a chosen role or user so you can test RLS.
Admin, Member, Contributor and Viewer: permission levels for everything in a workspace.
A Microsoft Purview label such as Confidential that classifies content and can protect exported files.

lessons.examTip: RLS restricts Viewers. People with Admin, Member or Contributor roles in the workspace can edit content and are not limited by RLS.

steps: Download staff.csv, staff-campus.csv, rls-roles.txt and security-matrix.md, and read the security matrix.
In Power BI Desktop, open Modeling and choose Manage roles. Create roles North, South and City, each filtering Tickets[Campus] with the filters in rls-roles.txt. Save.
Choose View as, tick the North role and check that every visual shows only North tickets. Then stop viewing.
Get data from staff.csv and name the table Staff. In Model view relate Staff[AssignedTo] 1 → * Tickets[AssignedTo] with single direction.

Create a role named Own Tickets with the filter [Email] = USERPRINCIPALNAME() on Staff. Use View as with Other user set to anu.sebastian@staff.example.edu plus the Own Tickets role, and check the visuals.

Get data from staff-campus.csv and name it StaffCampus. Delete any relationship Desktop creates for it, then create the Campus Lead role on Tickets from rls-roles.txt. Test it as divya.nair@staff.example.edu and as suresh.kumar@staff.example.edu.
Publish to your workspace. In the service, open the semantic model’s Security page and add yourself (or a group) as a member of the North role. Use Test as role.
Open Manage access on the workspace and review the four roles against security-matrix.md. Then share the report with a colleague and look at the permission options.
Apply a sensitivity label to the report in Desktop or the service, if labels are available in your tenant.
check: View as North shows 21 tickets; South shows 25 and City 14. If North shows 20, the Campus cleaning from B.4 is missing.
Own Tickets as anu.sebastian@staff.example.edu shows 13 tickets (8 Closed, 4 Open, 1 In progress); as joseph.mathew@staff.example.edu it shows 17.
Campus Lead as divya.nair@staff.example.edu shows 14 tickets (City only); as suresh.kumar@staff.example.edu it shows all 60.
Test as role North in the service shows the same 21 tickets as in Desktop.

quiz.question: Each Campus lead should see only their own Campus tickets. There are three campuses and the list of leads rarely changes. Which is the simplest correct setup?
options: Three static RLS roles, one per Campus, with members assigned in the service
Three copies of the report, one per Campus
Page-level filters on each report page
A sensitivity label for each Campus
quiz.explanation: Static RLS with one role per Campus filters the rows in the model. Page filters can be changed by users and copies are hard to maintain.

quiz.question: The Help Desk will grow to hundreds of agents. Each should see only tickets assigned to them, without creating a role per person. What should you use?
options: A Viewer role for each agent
One role that filters a staff table with USERPRINCIPALNAME()
quiz.explanation: Dynamic RLS uses one role. USERPRINCIPALNAME() returns the signed-in user, and a mapping table links that user to the rows they may see.

quiz.question: You set up RLS and added a manager to the workspace as a Member. The manager still sees all rows. Why?
options: USERPRINCIPALNAME() does not work in the service
RLS only restricts users with the Viewer role; Admin, Member and Contributor are not limited
RLS must be enabled in the tenant each day
Members need a sensitivity label first
quiz.explanation: RLS applies to people who only have read access, such as Viewers or app users. Editing roles in the workspace are not restricted by RLS.

quiz.question: Before publishing, you want to confirm that the North role only returns North tickets. What should you do in Power BI Desktop?
options: Publish to web and check the link
Assign the role to yourself in Desktop
Use View as and select the North role
quiz.explanation: View as in Desktop previews the report as one or more roles, or as another user for dynamic RLS. Members are assigned later in the service.

questionBank.question: The data team has published a certified Sales semantic model. You need to build a new report on the same data without importing or copying it again. What should you do in Power BI Desktop?
options: Get data from Power BI semantic models and connect live to the published model
Export the model's tables to CSV files and import them
Open a copy of the original .pbix file and delete its report pages
Use Analyze in Excel, save the workbook, then import the workbook
questionBank.explanation: Connecting to a published Power BI semantic model creates a live connection: the report reuses the single trusted model and nothing is copied. The other options create duplicate, unmanaged copies of the data.

questionBank.question: Twelve queries read from a SQL Server. The server name is different in test and production. You want to switch environments by changing one value, also after publishing. What should you do?
options: Create a calculated table that lists both server names
Create a Power Query parameter for the server name and use it in each query's Source step
Create a what-if parameter and bind it to a slicer
Duplicate every query, one set per environment
questionBank.explanation: A Power Query parameter can be referenced in the Source step of every query, and its value can be changed in Power Query or later in the semantic model settings in the service. What-if parameters are for DAX scenarios, not connections.

questionBank.question: The password for a database account changed. Refreshing in Power BI Desktop now fails with a credentials error. Where do you update the stored credentials?
options: Delete the queries and import the tables again
Open Performance Analyzer and select Refresh visuals
File > Options and settings > Data source settings, select the source, then Edit Permissions
In Model view, open the table properties and change the storage mode
questionBank.explanation: Data source settings hold the credentials and privacy level for each source. Edit Permissions lets you replace the credentials without rebuilding any queries.

questionBank.question: In Power Query you want to see the minimum, maximum, average, standard deviation and null count for HoursToResolve. Which data preview option shows these statistics?
questionBank.explanation: Column profile shows column statistics (count, errors, empty, distinct, min, max, average, standard deviation and more) plus a value distribution chart. Column quality only shows valid, error and empty percentages; column distribution shows distinct and unique counts.

questionBank.question: Some tickets have a null Priority. The business rule is that a missing priority means Medium. You want the fix applied once, before the data reaches the model. What should you do in Power Query?
options: Remove rows where Priority is null
Use Replace Values on Priority to replace null with Medium
Use Fill Down on the Priority column
Change the Priority column type to Whole Number
questionBank.explanation: Replace Values swaps null for Medium in every row and keeps all tickets. Removing rows loses data, and Fill Down copies the value from the row above, which is only correct when blank means "same as previous".

questionBank.question: After you select Close & Apply, Power BI Desktop reports that a table loaded with some errors. You need to see exactly which rows caused them. What should you do?
options: Select View errors to open a query that lists the rows with errors, then fix the cause
Change the column data type in the Model view
Turn off Enable load for the table
Delete the table and load the CSV file again
questionBank.explanation: View errors creates an error query in Power Query that shows the affected rows and the error details, so you can fix the step or source value that caused them. Reloading or disabling load does not find the cause.

questionBank.question: A web API returns JSON: a list of records, and each record holds ticket fields. In Power Query you see a single List. How do you turn it into a normal table with one column per field?
options: Pivot the column on the field names
Convert the list To Table, then use the expand button to expand the record fields into columns
Split the column by the delimiter "{"
questionBank.explanation: Semi-structured data is flattened by converting the list to a table and then expanding the record (or nested list) columns. Splitting text or pivoting does not understand the JSON structure.

questionBank.question: You suspect some tickets have a CategoryID that does not exist in the Categories table. In Power Query you want a list of only those orphan tickets. Which merge join kind should you use with Tickets as the first table?
questionBank.explanation: A left anti join keeps only the rows from the first table that have no match in the second table, which is exactly the list of orphan tickets. Inner keeps only matches; left outer keeps everything.

questionBank.question: A report only needs ticket counts and average resolution hours per Campus and month, never individual tickets. You want to shrink the loaded table. What should you use in Power Query?
options: Group By on Campus and Month with Count Rows and Average of HoursToResolve
questionBank.explanation: Group By aggregates rows to the grain the report needs, which reduces rows and model size. Pivot and transpose reshape data but do not aggregate it to a lower grain.

questionBank.question: A composite model has a large Sales fact table in DirectQuery. The small Date and Product tables are used by slicers that filter both DirectQuery and imported tables. Which storage mode is usually best for Date and Product?
questionBank.explanation: Dual tables can act as Import or DirectQuery depending on the query, so they filter imported tables from memory and can join to DirectQuery tables at the source. Direct Lake applies to Fabric OneLake data, not this composite scenario.

questionBank.question: A Budget table and a Targets table are both at Campus and Month grain; no single column is unique. You need a one-to-one or one-to-many relationship between them. What should you do?
options: Create two active relationships, one on Campus and one on Month
Set the relationship cardinality to many-to-many on Campus
In Power Query, create a key column that combines Campus and Month in both tables and relate on it
Append the two tables into one table
questionBank.explanation: A model relationship links one column to one column, so a composite key column (for example Campus and Month merged) gives each row a unique value to relate on. Two active relationships between the same tables are not allowed.

questionBank.question: You need a measure that returns how many different agents handled tickets in the current filter context. Which expression is correct?
questionBank.explanation: DISTINCTCOUNT counts unique values. COUNT and COUNTROWS count every ticket, so an agent with ten tickets is counted ten times; SUM cannot add text.

questionBank.question: A matrix shows Campus on rows and Priority on columns. Each cell must show that priority's share of its campus total. Which denominator should you use in DIVIDE([Total Tickets], …)?
questionBank.explanation: REMOVEFILTERS on the Priority column clears only the priority filter, so the campus filter stays and the denominator is the campus total. ALL(Tickets) removes the campus filter too and gives the grand total.

questionBank.question:
You write:
Closed = CALCULATE([Total Tickets], USERELATIONSHIP(Tickets[ClosedDate], 'Date'[Date]))
The measure fails, saying there is no relationship between the columns. What is the cause?
options: USERELATIONSHIP only works inside a calculated column
USERELATIONSHIP activates an existing relationship; you must first create the (inactive) relationship between ClosedDate and Date
The Date table must use Both cross-filter direction
ClosedDate must be the active relationship before USERELATIONSHIP is used
questionBank.explanation: USERELATIONSHIP does not create a relationship. It turns on an existing inactive one for the duration of the CALCULATE, so the inactive ClosedDate to Date relationship must exist in the model.

questionBank.question: You need a measure that shows tickets created from 1 January up to the date in the current filter context, restarting each year. Your Date table is marked as a date table. Which filter do you place in CALCULATE([Total Tickets], …)?
questionBank.explanation: DATESYTD returns the dates from the start of the year to the last date in context, giving a year-to-date total. SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR, DATEADD and PARALLELPERIOD shift the period instead.

questionBank.question:
Consider:
YoY % = VAR PY = CALCULATE([Total Tickets], SAMEPERIODLASTYEAR('Date'[Date])) RETURN DIVIDE([Total Tickets] - PY, PY)
The Help Desk data only covers 2026. What does the measure show for March 2026?
options: An error, because the prior-year value is missing
0%, because blank is treated as zero in the result
100%, because the current value is divided by itself
Blank, because DIVIDE returns blank when the denominator is blank or zero
questionBank.explanation: There are no 2025 tickets, so PY is blank. DIVIDE returns BLANK (or an optional alternate result) instead of an error when the denominator is blank or zero.

questionBank.question: HoursToResolve is skewed by a few tickets that took a very long time. The manager wants a "typical" resolution time that these few tickets do not pull upward. Which measure is best?
questionBank.explanation: The median is the middle value, so a few extreme values affect it much less than the average. STDEV.P measures spread, not a typical value.

questionBank.question: The manager wants the average of each agent's total resolution hours (not the average per ticket). Which measure is correct?
questionBank.explanation: AVERAGEX iterates the list of agents, computes each agent's total (CALCULATE turns the row into a filter), then averages those totals. The other options work per ticket or just add everything up.

questionBank.question:
What does this measure return?
CALCULATE([Total Tickets], Tickets[Priority] = "High", Tickets[Status] <> "Closed")
options: Tickets that are High priority or not closed
An error, because CALCULATE accepts only one filter
High priority tickets that are not closed
questionBank.explanation: Multiple filter arguments in CALCULATE are combined with AND, so the result counts tickets that are High priority and whose status is not Closed.

questionBank.question: Users need a slicer that groups tickets into Fast, Standard and Slow based on each ticket's HoursToResolve. What should you create?
options: A calculated column that uses SWITCH (or a conditional column in Power Query)
questionBank.explanation: Slicers need a column with a value on each row. A calculated column (or a Power Query conditional column) stores the band per ticket; measures and calculation groups cannot be used as slicer values this way.

questionBank.question: You built a Date table with CALENDARAUTO. You want time intelligence to use it and to stop Power BI creating hidden date tables for every date column. What should you do?
options: Mark the table as a date table using its Date column, and turn off Auto date/time in Options
Set the Date column's data category to Address
Relate the Date table to Tickets with Both cross-filter direction
Convert the Date table to DirectQuery
questionBank.explanation: Marking a table as a date table tells Power BI which column to use for time intelligence; turning off Auto date/time stops the hidden automatic date tables and keeps the model smaller.

questionBank.question: Report authors keep dragging TicketID into visuals, and it appears as a meaningless sum. What is the best model fix?
options: Set the TicketID column's summarization to Don't summarize
Set Sort by column on TicketID
questionBank.explanation: Default summarization is a column property. Setting it to Don't summarize stops numeric ID columns from being added up automatically when placed in a visual.

questionBank.question: A semantic model imports ten years of ticket history, but every report only looks at the last two years. Refresh is slow and the model is large. What is the best change?
options: Set all relationships to Both cross-filter direction
Add a report-level filter for the last two years
Filter the rows in Power Query so only the needed years are loaded
Change every visual to a table visual
questionBank.explanation: Removing unneeded rows before load reduces model size and refresh time. A report-level filter hides the rows but they are still imported and stored.

questionBank.question: You need one visual that starts with open tickets at the start of the month, adds new tickets, subtracts closed tickets and ends with open tickets at month end. Which visual fits best?
questionBank.explanation: A waterfall chart shows a running total as values are added and subtracted from a starting value, which matches the start, increases, decreases and end story.

questionBank.question: A manager wants a short written summary on the report page that updates when slicers change, generated by Copilot. Copilot is enabled for the workspace. What should you add?
questionBank.explanation: The narrative visual with Copilot writes a summary of the visuals on the page or report and can be refreshed as filters change. A text box is static, and Q&A answers typed questions.

questionBank.question: In a single line chart you want a running total of tickets by month, defined only on that visual without adding a measure to the semantic model. What should you use?
options: A visual calculation such as RUNNINGSUM([Total Tickets])
A quick measure for running total
questionBank.explanation: Visual calculations are DAX defined on a visual and computed over its data, so functions like RUNNINGSUM work without adding anything to the model. A quick measure creates a model measure.

questionBank.question: One bar chart must show only the three agents with the most tickets. Other visuals on the page must show all agents. What should you do?
options: Add a Basic filter on AssignedTo at the page level
Add a report-level filter on AssignedTo
Add a visual-level filter on AssignedTo with filter type Top N, showing the top 3 by Total Tickets
Add a slicer on AssignedTo and select three agents
questionBank.explanation: A visual-level Top N filter affects only that visual and updates automatically as the ranking changes. Page and report filters, or a slicer, affect other visuals too.

questionBank.question: Users want a button to switch between a chart view and a table view in the same space on a page. What should you use?
options: Edit interactions between the two visuals
Two bookmarks that capture visual visibility from the Selection pane, linked to buttons
questionBank.explanation: Bookmarks can store which visuals are shown or hidden (set in the Selection pane). Buttons with a bookmark action switch between those states.

questionBank.question: When users hover over a bar for a campus, they should see a small chart of that campus's tickets by priority. What should you set up?
options: A report page with Allow use as tooltip turned on, then select that page in the bar chart's tooltip settings
Conditional formatting on the bar chart
questionBank.explanation: Report page tooltips are built on a separate page marked for tooltip use and then assigned to a visual. They show filtered to the data point being hovered.

questionBank.question: Some report users rely on a screen reader and keyboard navigation. Which two settings help them most?
options: A dark theme and larger page size
Alt text on each visual and a logical tab order set in the Selection pane
Auto page refresh and data alerts
questionBank.explanation: Alt text lets screen readers describe visuals, and tab order in the Selection pane controls the order keyboard users move through them. Also avoid using colour alone to carry meaning.

questionBank.question: Most managers open the Help Desk report on their phones and must scroll and zoom to read it. What should you do in Power BI Desktop?
options: Reduce the page size to letter
Publish the report as a paginated report
Open Mobile layout view and arrange the key visuals for portrait phone screens
questionBank.explanation: Mobile layout lets you place and size visuals for a portrait phone canvas; the Power BI mobile app uses it when the report is opened on a phone.

questionBank.question: A line chart shows daily ticket counts. You want Power BI to highlight unusual spikes or drops automatically and show possible explanations. What should you use?
options: Error bars in the Analytics pane
A constant line at the average
Find anomalies (anomaly detection) in the Analytics pane
questionBank.explanation: Anomaly detection on a line chart marks points outside the expected range and can show possible explanations based on other fields. Clusters apply to scatter charts and tables.

questionBank.question: You have a scatter chart of agents with ticket count on one axis and average hours on the other. You want Power BI to group similar agents automatically. What should you use?
options: Automatically find clusters on the scatter chart
questionBank.explanation: Automatically find clusters groups similar data points in a scatter chart and creates a cluster field you can reuse. Binning splits one numeric column into equal ranges.

questionBank.question: The manager wants to break total tickets down step by step by Campus, then Category, then Priority, choosing the order freely and letting AI suggest the highest split. Which visual fits best?
questionBank.explanation: The decomposition tree lets users drill a measure through dimensions in any order and includes AI splits that pick the highest or lowest value. Key influencers explains what drives an outcome instead.

questionBank.question: A colleague must publish, edit and delete content in the Help Desk workspace, but must not add or remove people from the workspace. Which workspace role should you assign?
questionBank.explanation: Contributors can create, edit and delete content but cannot manage workspace access. Members can add people with lower permissions, and Viewers can only view.

questionBank.question: The service desk lead wants the Overview report page emailed to her every Monday morning, without logging in first. What should you set up?
options: A data alert on a dashboard tile
An email subscription to the report page with a weekly Monday schedule
questionBank.explanation: Subscriptions send a snapshot and link of a report page or dashboard by email on a schedule. Data alerts fire only when a tile value crosses a threshold.

questionBank.question: You plan scheduled refresh in the Power BI service for several semantic models. Which source requires an on-premises data gateway?
options: A SQL Server database on a server in the company's server room
An Azure SQL Database that allows public network access
questionBank.explanation: A gateway is needed when the service must reach data inside a private, on-premises network. Cloud sources reachable from the service, such as SharePoint Online, public Azure SQL and Dataverse, do not need one.

questionBank.question: A report contains confidential HR ticket data. The label must travel with the data when users export it to Excel, PowerPoint or PDF. What should you apply?
options: A Microsoft Purview sensitivity label such as Confidential
A separate workspace with Viewer access only
questionBank.explanation: Sensitivity labels from Microsoft Purview Information Protection classify content and, for supported exports, the label and its protection go with the exported file. Endorsement signals trust, not confidentiality.

questionBank.question: An analyst in the Finance workspace wants to build her own reports on the Help Desk semantic model, but must not get access to the Help Desk workspace. What should you grant?
options: The Viewer role in the Help Desk workspace
The Contributor role in the Help Desk workspace
Build permission on the Help Desk semantic model
questionBank.explanation: Build permission on a semantic model lets a user create new reports on it from their own workspace or Desktop without any workspace role. RLS roles restrict rows but do not grant build rights.

questionBank.question: The North campus RLS role currently lists 25 individual users, and staff move between campuses often. You want less maintenance. What should you do?
options: Create one RLS role per user
Give each North user the Member workspace role
Replace the role filter with USERPRINCIPALNAME() in a calculated column
Add a Microsoft Entra security group to the role in the service and manage membership in that group
questionBank.explanation: RLS role membership accepts security groups. When people move, only group membership changes, and the Power BI role stays the same.
